  - 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son ... I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father." David's son and God's son appear in one verse.
  - Acts 13:33: "he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee."
  - Romans 1:4: "declared to be the Son of God with power ... by the resurrection from the dead." It is joined to Romans 1:3, "of the seed of David according to the flesh."

Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20 ("of the Holy Ghost") are answered at Link 1.

**LINK 5: NARROWED TO:** Isaiah's sign is bounded in Isaiah's own day, and Isaiah 8:3-4 records a child conceived under the same bound after the prophet "went unto the prophetess." I drop any claim that the two names are one.

Footing:
- **[L1] The bound on the sign.** Isaiah 7:16: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings."
- **[L1] The same bound on Isaiah's child.** Isaiah 8:4: "before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away."
- **[L1] How that child came.** Isaiah 8:3: "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son." The margin reads "Heb. approached."
- **[L1] Immanuel in Isaiah's day.** Isaiah 8:8: "the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel."
- **[L2] The two words for Rebekah.** The clause "neither had any man known her" stands with *bethulah* (virgin) at Genesis 24:16. *Almah* (young woman) at Genesis 24:43 carries no such clause.
- **[L3] Matthew's "fulfilled."** Matthew 1:22-23 stands as written. "Fulfilled" applies an earlier word, as Matthew 2:15 applies Hosea 11:1's "called my son out of Egypt," spoken first of Israel.

Isaiah 7:11, "ask it either in the depth, or in the height above," is the sign offered to Ahaz. Isaiah 7:16 bounds that same sign.

**LINK 6: NARROWED TO:** the signet the LORD swore to pluck from Coniah, he set on Coniah's grandson, so the LORD answers his own pronounced sentence on the line.

Footing:
- **[L1] The sentence.** Jeremiah 22:24: "though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence."
- **[L1] The line continues.** Matthew 1:12: "Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel."
- **[L1] The signet set again.** Haggai 2:23: "O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel ... will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee."

  - Jeremiah 18:7 speaks of his word "to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy."

I grant that Haggai seats Zerubbabel on no throne. Jeremiah 22:30, "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David," stands as written. The throne comes as the LORD's gift: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32). The giver of that throne is the One who pronounced the sentence and set the signet again.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 4, CLOSE ROUND

# CLOSE ROUND: Defender

I keep D1, D2 and D4. I narrow D3, D5 and the Isaiah limb of D1. I name where footing is thin and do not rest weight there. Nothing new is pressed.

---

## D1: Mary was a virgin when she conceived. NARROWED TO: the limb that stands on Luke 1:27, Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:18–25. Isaiah 7:14 corroborates and is not load-bearing.

- [L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." The Greek *parthenos* means "virgin."
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Genesis 4:1 sets the text's own sense of *ginōskō* ("to know"): "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."
- [L2] *Parthenos* is Matthew's word in Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child."
- [L3] On Genesis 24:16 and 24:43 the challenger's point stands in part. The clause "neither had any man known her" sits with *bethulah* ("virgin") in Genesis 24:16. I do not rest weight on *ʿalmāh* ("young woman") alone. Genesis 24:43 does apply the KJV's "virgin" to the very Rebekah of Genesis 24:16, but the Greek of Matthew 1:23 and Luke 1:34 carry the load.

**C5 and the Isaiah witnesses.**

ANSWER: Isaiah 8:3-4 -- D1 -- "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son." And: "For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria."
- [L1] This child was conceived by ordinary approach (margin: "Heb. approached").
- [L1] The LORD gives him a different name: "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz" (Isaiah 8:3). Isaiah 7:14 says "shall call his name Immanuel."
- I grant a near referent may share the time bound of Isaiah 7:16. That does not touch Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:18, which state Mary's virginity in their own words.

ANSWER: Isaiah 7:11 -- D1 -- "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above."
- [L1] Isaiah 7:14 begins "the Lord himself shall give you a sign." The sign offered in 7:11 is of the deep or the height.
- [L4] Footing: Isaiah 7:11 (a sign from the deep or the height) and Isaiah 8:3 (an ordinary conception "by approach" that needs no sign). The chain: a conception by approach is no such sign, so the sign of 7:14 is better met by what Matthew records than by Isaiah 8:3.
- I do not claim more than "better met." The close of D1 rests on the Luke and Matthew rows.

ANSWER: Matthew 1:22-23 -- D1 -- "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel."
- [L1] "All this" is the whole of Matthew 1:18–21: found with child of the Holy Ghost, before they came together, Joseph not knowing her.
- Matthew says the virgin conception is what was "done" and fulfils the word. The challenger's own point, that "fulfilled" can apply an earlier word, leaves that standing.

ANSWER: Matthew 2:15 -- D1 -- "And was there until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son."
ANSWER: Hosea 11:1 -- D1 -- "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt."
- [L1] Hosea 11:1 speaks first of Israel. Matthew 2:15 says "fulfilled" of Jesus.
- [L4] Footing: Matthew 2:15 with Hosea 11:1 (a word spoken of an earlier child, applied by Matthew to Jesus), and Matthew 1:22 (the same "fulfilled" formula over the conception). The chain: if the formula allows a prior referent in Hosea, a prior referent in Isaiah does not remove Matthew's application in 1:23.
- I concede the formula does not by itself prove virginity from Isaiah. It only removes the objection that Isaiah's own day forbids Matthew's use.

**C1 (the claim that Joseph knew Mary within the espousal). I answer from the text.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." The pregnancy is found before coming together.
- [L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." A husband who knew her would have no cause to be minded to put her away.
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Here *gar* ("for") gives the ground for removing his fear. That ground answers a suspicion of fault, not a question of who the father was.
- [L4] Footing: Matthew 1:19 (Joseph's intent to put her away) and Matthew 1:18–20 (the angel's reason of the Holy Ghost). The chain: only if Joseph had not known her does the angel's reason meet his trouble. Deuteronomy 22:24 calls a betrothed damsel "wife," and Matthew 1:20 does the same. It does not follow that union had occurred, because Matthew 1:24 still has Joseph "took unto him his wife" afterward.

---

## D2: The stated source is the Holy Ghost, and Joseph did not know her until the birth. KEPT.

- [L1] Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source.
- [L2] The KJV margin at Matthew 1:20 reads "Gr. begotten." The Greek *gennēthen* means "begotten." The thing begotten in her is *ek pneumatos hagiou* ("out of the Holy Spirit").
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." The Greek *eginōsken* is imperfect: he was not knowing her. Genesis 4:1 gives the sequence of knowing, then conceiving. Matthew 1:25 says no knowing came before the birth.

**On the challenger's "ek + God" reading.**
- [L1] 1 John 5:1: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God."
- That verse speaks of those already born of earthly parents. Matthew 1:20 says "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The object is the conceived thing in the womb, so the *ek* names the source of the conceiving.

**On Matthew 1:25 "till."** I claim only the span up to the birth. "Till" fixes the end of the knowing-not, and I draw nothing from after it.

**On Luke 1:35.** The challenger reads "born of thee" as naming only the bearer. Granted: it names the bearer, as Luke 1:13 does for Elisabeth. D2 does not rest on it.

---

## D3: The child was brought into being by divine power, and the human origin is the woman alone. NARROWED TO: Luke 1:34–35 as one question and answer. Galatians 4:4 and Genesis 3:15 are corroboration only.

- [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
- [L4] Footing: Luke 1:34 (the question, "seeing I know not a man") and Luke 1:35 (the answer in terms of the Holy Ghost and power, naming no man). The chain: the answer is given to the question "how," so it gives the means of conceiving where no man is involved.
- [L3] Exodus 40:35, "the cloud abode thereon, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The overshadowing is the LORD's presence in power. I do not say the verb itself means generation.

**Concessions.**
- Galatians 4:4, "made of a woman," says what Job 14:1 and Matthew 11:11 say of every mortal. Taken alone it excludes nothing about a father. It names the woman as the human source and stays beside Luke 1:35.
- Genesis 3:15, "her seed," is matched by Genesis 16:10 and Genesis 24:60. It is not load-bearing and I withdraw it from the weight.

**C3.** On Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son," the challenger's reading is accepted as far as it goes. The speaker addresses the mother, and I do not argue from the absence of "bear thee."

**C4.**

ANSWER: Luke 9:34-35 -- D3 -- "While he thus spake, there came a cloud, and overshadowed them: and they feared as they entered into the cloud. And there came a voice out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son: hear him."
- [L1] The cloud overshadows "them," the disciples as well as Jesus, and no generation is in view. I grant the verb means presence.
- [L4] Footing: Luke 1:34–35 (the verb's setting as the answer to "I know not a man") and Luke 9:34 (a use of the verb with no generation). The chain: the verb alone does not prove generation, but in Luke 1 its context does.

ANSWER: Luke 9:35 -- D3 -- "And there came a voice out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son: hear him."
- [L1] The voice declares sonship over a grown man. It does not say a man did not beget him.
- I do not rest D3 on the word "Son" alone.

ANSWER: Hebrews 7:5 -- D3 -- "though they come out of the loins of Abraham."
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10 says of Levi: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." Levi was in the loins of Abraham, his great-grandfather. The word "loins" reaches across generations, so a descendant's seed is in the forefather's loins.
- [L1] Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh." Psalms 132:11: "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne."
- [L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- [L4] Footing: Romans 1:3 (the child is seed of David according to the flesh), Luke 1:31 and 1:35 (the child is conceived in and born of Mary alone), and Galatians 4:4 (made of a woman). The chain: if the flesh is Mary's alone, then the seed of David is through Mary.
- I grant the KJV text never states Mary's descent. That is an inference from Romans 1:3, resting on D3's own premise that Mary is the sole human source. It is not independent proof of D3.

---

## D4: Joseph's fatherhood is legal and supposed, not generative. KEPT.

- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] The Greek verb *egennēsen* ("begat") is repeated through the whole list. At the last link the text changes to the passive *egennēthē* ("was born") with the relative *hēs* ("of whom," feminine singular). The father's active verb stops before the last name.
- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- [L1] Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Luke 2:49 is the answer: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

ANSWER: Matthew 1:3 -- D4 -- "And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begat Esrom; and Esrom begat Aram."
- [L1] Matthew 1:3 shows the pattern: "A begat B." The mother appears with "of," and the verb belongs to the father. Matthew 1:16 does not follow it: it says "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
- [L4] Footing: Matthew 1:3 (the active father pattern) and Matthew 1:16 (the break to the passive with feminine "of whom"). The chain: the repeated pattern is exactly what Matthew 1:16 breaks, and the break puts the birth on Mary.
- I concede the passive does not itself narrate the begetting. I rely on the break together with Matthew 1:18–25 (D2).

**On Luke 3:23.**
- I concede *enomizeto* can have the milder sense "was wont" (Acts 16:13).
- In Luke 3:23 the KJV gives "(as was supposed)," and *hōs* ("as") marks it as opinion. Luke's own record in Luke 1:34–35 and Luke 2:48–49 sets the supposed and the stated side by side.
- Mary's "thy father" is the common speech of the household. It is not the narrator's verdict.

---

## D5: The royal line fits this. NARROWED TO: the line fits and corroborates. It does not prove the premise, and D1–D4 do not rest on it.

- [L1] Jeremiah 22:30: "Write ye this man childless... for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah."
- [L1] Matthew 1:12 puts Joseph's line in the descent through Jechonias: "Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel."
- [L1] Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."

**C6.**
- The challenger points to Jeremiah 22:24 and Haggai 2:23: "will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee, saith the LORD of hosts."
- I concede Haggai 2:23 sets Zerubbabel as a signet and not on a throne.

ANSWER: Jeremiah 18:7 -- D5 -- "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it."
- [L1] Jeremiah 18:8 gives the condition: "If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them."
- The condition is that the nation turns. Jeremiah 22:30 states no condition. No verse says Coniah's seed turned, and none says the sentence was repealed.
- [L4] Footing: Jeremiah 22:30 with 22:24 (a sentence given "As I live") and Jeremiah 18:7–8 (repentance tied to turning, which the record does not show). The chain: the general rule does not by itself remove this specific sentence.
- I concede the rule means the LORD could answer his own sentence. D5 says the sentence fits Luke 1:32's throne "given" by the Lord God. It does not prove how.

**C2.**
- I concede the text names Joseph as of David's house (Luke 1:27, Luke 2:4) and that the reckoning runs by the father's house (Numbers 1:18, Hebrews 7:14).
- I drop any claim that Mary's own house is stated. Her only named kin are Aaronic: Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:5.
- I keep this: Joseph's place in David's house and his legal fatherhood (D4) give the child the legal line. Romans 1:3 gives the flesh through the woman (see D3). Nothing in these rows requires a begetting by Joseph.

---

## D6: Therefore Christ had no biological father. KEPT, resting on D1, D2 and D4, with D3 narrowed as above.

- [L1] Luke 1:27 and 1:34: Mary a virgin, not knowing a man.
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: found with child of the Holy Ghost before coming together.
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L1] Matthew 1:16 and Luke 3:23: Joseph is husband and supposed father.
- [L4] Footing: Matthew 1:18–25 (conceived of the Holy Ghost, Joseph not knowing her) together with Luke 1:34–35 (a conception answered "how" without a man). The chain: the only source named for the conceiving is the Holy Ghost, and the only man named is excluded from knowing Mary until the birth. Therefore the text gives no biological father.

I rest here. The challenger's points on the verbs *episkiasei* ("will overshadow") and *enomizeto* ("was supposed"), on Galatians 4:4, and on the ground of Isaiah's day are accepted as limits on those words. They do not reach Luke 1:34–35 or Matthew 1:18–25, the stated rows on which the case stands.

The case I made: **Christ had a biological father, and the man the text names is Joseph, of the house of David.** I rest on the rows already pressed. I press nothing new. I keep my links under C1–C6.

---

## The keystone

The seed sworn to David comes out of a man's body, and the text names one man of David's house as the child's father.

- [L1] 2 Samuel 7:12 says the seed is from David's own body: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
- [L1] Psalms 132:11 says the same: "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne." The margin reads "Heb. belly."
- [L1] Acts 2:30 applies it to the Christ: "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
- [L1] Romans 1:3 calls him "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- [L1] Hebrews 7:14 says this was plain to see: "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10 shows whose loins carry the seed: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." The loins in these rows are a father's loins.

## C1: SUPPORTED. Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal.

- **Footing [L1]:** The seed rows above require seed out of a man's loins.
- **Footing [L1]:** Genesis 4:1 gives the text's own means of begetting: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."
- **Footing [L1]:** Joseph and Mary were husband and wife from the espousal. Matthew 1:19 says "Joseph her husband." Matthew 1:20 says "Mary thy wife." Deuteronomy 22:24 calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife."
- **[L4] Chain:** The promise requires seed out of a man's loins. The text's means is a husband knowing his wife. The one man named is the husband from the espousal, of David's house. So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins.

**The timing rows, held as written and read inside the chain:**

- [L1] Matthew 1:18 dates when the pregnancy was found: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." The verb can name married union, as in 1 Corinthians 7:5: "come together again."
- [L1] Matthew 1:24 then says what came together: "took unto him his wife." This is her coming into his house.
- [L1] Matthew 1:25 follows that taking: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." Its span is the pregnancy after the taking, bounded by "till."
- [L2] Luke 1:34, "seeing I know not a man," is *andra ou ginōskō* ("a man I do not know"). The verb is present indicative. It states her condition when the angel spoke. It is not a vow.
- [L2] Matthew 1:19 has *dikaios ōn* ("being just") and *mē thelōn autēn paradeigmatisai* ("not willing to make her an example"). These are Joseph's intent and its two stated grounds. The verse has no verb of knowing. The defender's cause for that intent is the defender's own inference.

**The angel's "for":**

- [L1] Matthew 1:20 says "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] Here *ek* ("of, out of") with the Spirit names covenant origin. 1 John 5:1 uses the same "of" for people with earthly parents: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God." The defender's own answer granted this point: being "of God" stands beside earthly birth.
- [L3] 1 Chronicles 28:6 puts both in one verse: "Solomon thy son ... for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father." David's son and God's son are the same man in the same verse.

---

## C2: NARROWED TO the named rows. Joseph alone is placed in David's house, and the reckoning runs by the father's house.

- [L1] Luke 1:27 places Joseph in David's house: "a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."
- [L1] Luke 2:4 repeats it: "he was of the house and lineage of David."
- [L1] Numbers 1:2 gives the rule of reckoning: "by the house of their fathers." Numbers 1:18 says they "declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."
- [L1] Ezra 2:61–62 shows the reverse case. A man who "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name" was "as polluted, put from the priesthood."
- [L1] Mary's only named kin is Elisabeth (Luke 1:36). Elisabeth is "of the daughters of Aaron" (Luke 1:5).

The defender conceded that Mary's house is never stated. The defender also called D3's flesh-through-Mary "not independent proof of D3." So the seed of David according to the flesh has one named route: the man of David's house.

---

## C3: SUPPORTED. "Made of a woman" is said of every mortal.

- [L1] Galatians 4:4 says "made of a woman."
- [L3] Job 14:1 says "Man that is born of a woman is of few days."
- [L3] Matthew 11:11 says this of John, whose father is named in Luke 1:13: "Among them that are born of women."

The defender withdrew both Galatians 4:4 and Genesis 3:15 from the weight. That leaves D3 resting on Luke 1:34–35 alone.

## C4: SUPPORTED. The angel's verbs name presence and power.

The defender granted that the verb means presence. The defender then rested on Luke 1's context. That context is a Davidic throne "of his father David."

---

## C5: NARROWED TO Isaiah's own day.

- [L1] Isaiah 7:16 bounds the sign: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good."
- [L1] Isaiah 8:3–4 records a child conceived under that bound. Isaiah 8:3 says "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived." Isaiah 8:4 says "before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother."
- [L1] Isaiah 8:8 addresses Immanuel in that same day: "O Immanuel."
- I set no verse against Matthew 1:22–23. His "fulfilled" applies the earlier word, as Matthew 2:15 applies Hosea 11:1.

The defender conceded that the formula "does not by itself prove virginity from Isaiah." D1 now rests on Luke 1:27 and 1:34. Those rows state her condition at the espousal and when the angel spoke. Both stand as written, and C1's chain is not set against them.

---

## C6: NARROWED TO this point: the curse does not carry D5.

- [L1] Jeremiah 22:30 says "Write ye this man childless." Yet Matthew 1:12 records "Jechonias begat Salathiel."
- [L1] Jeremiah 22:24 says "yet would I pluck thee thence." Haggai 2:23 says the LORD "will make thee as a signet" of Zerubbabel.
- [L1] Jeremiah 18:8 states the LORD's own rule for a sentence he has pronounced: "I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them."

The defender narrowed D5 to "fits and corroborates" and said D1–D4 do not rest on it.

---

## D4 and the father named

- [L1] Matthew 1:16 names Joseph "the husband of Mary." The defender conceded "the passive does not itself narrate the begetting."
- [L1] The narrator calls them "the parents" (Luke 2:27) and "his parents" (Luke 2:41). Luke 2:33 says "Joseph and his mother."
- [L1] This is the narrator's own voice, not only household speech. Mary also says "thy father and I" (Luke 2:48).
- [L1] Luke 2:49's "my Father's business" is the covenant Father of 1 Chronicles 28:6, "I will be his father." That verse says it of a son David begat.
- [L2] In Luke 3:23, *enomizeto* ("was supposed") is the same form as Acts 16:13: "where prayer was wont to be made." The defender conceded it can carry that sense.
- [L1] The town says "the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know" (John 6:42). A disciple says "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45).

---

## UNSUPPORTED-L4 PREMISES (defender's words, verbatim)

1. **LINK D6:** "the only man named is excluded from knowing Mary until the birth."
   - [L1] Matthew 1:24–25 shows the span: "took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." The knowing-not follows the taking. It is not shown before the taking.

2. **LINK D2:** "Matthew 1:25 says no knowing came before the birth."
   - [L1] The same rows answer it. The verse covers the pregnancy after Matthew 1:24.

3. **LINK D3:** "The chain: if the flesh is Mary's alone, then the seed of David is through Mary."
   - The defender's own words answer it: "I grant the KJV text never states Mary's descent."
   - [L1] Luke 1:5 and 1:36 name her only kin as Aaronic. Numbers 1:2 reckons "by the house of their fathers." The premise is circular.

4. **LINK D2/D6:** "A husband who knew her would have no cause to be minded to put her away."
   - [L2] Matthew 1:19 gives intent and two grounds, "being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example." It has no verb of knowing.

---

## Final word

These rows hold together, and none needs to be set against another:

- The promise was sworn to David's loins, "according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30).
- The seed is "evident" (Hebrews 7:14).
- It is reckoned "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:2).
- The one man of that house the text names is "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19).
- Mary herself says "thy father and I" (Luke 2:48).
- "Of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20) is the "of" that 1 John 5:1 uses for people with earthly parents.
- "Son of God" is the title given beside "the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32).

On these rows, the child had a biological father, Joseph.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean the male parent whose seed, joined to the mother's, begets the child. The standard reading is that Christ had a mother, Mary, but no human male parent. His conception was the work of the Holy Ghost. Joseph was his legal and reputed father only.

## 1. Matthew's genealogy stops begetting at Joseph

[L1] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;" The pattern is a male who begat a male.

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] The verb in verse 2 is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, G1080 gennaō), meaning "begat, fathered." In verse 16 the pattern changes. Joseph is called "the husband (ἀνήρ, anēr, G435) of Mary," not the one who begat Jesus. The relative pronoun "of whom" is ἧς (hēs), which is feminine singular. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph or to both. The verb is ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē), "was born," which is passive.

[L3] Matthew 1:18 supports this: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

[L4] Matthew keeps "begat" for every earlier link (Matthew 1:2). In Matthew 1:16 he changes both the verb and the pronoun to the feminine singular "of whom." The grammar therefore deliberately cuts Joseph out as the begetter and names Mary alone as the one of whom Jesus was born.

## 2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost, before Joseph and Mary came together

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

[L2] "Of" in both verses is ἐκ (ek, G1537), meaning "out of, from the source of." "Conceived" is γεννηθέν (gennēthen, G1080), the same root as "begat." The origin of the begetting is therefore stated as the Holy Ghost. "Before they came together" is πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν (prin ē synelthein, G4905 synerchomai), meaning "to come together," which here means to unite as husband and wife. The conception was finished before that union.

[L3] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS." Joseph did not "know" (ἐγίνωσκεν, G1097 ginōskō, here used for marital knowledge) his wife until after the birth.

[L4] The text gives the source of the begetting (ἐκ, G1537, Matthew 1:20) as the Holy Ghost. It also says the couple did not unite until after the birth (Matthew 1:25). So no human male begot the child.

## 3. Mary herself, and the angel, say so

[L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." [L2] παρθένος (parthenos, G3933) means "virgin, a girl who has not had relations."

[L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" [L2] "Know" is ginōskō (G1097), the same word as in Matthew 1:25, used of relations between a man and a woman.

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L2] "Overshadow" is ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, G1982), meaning "to cast a shadow over, envelop." "Therefore" is διό (dio, G1352), meaning "for which reason." The cause is stated: the Holy Ghost comes upon her and the power of the Highest overshadows her. The result is stated as "that holy thing which shall be born of thee." The source of the child is in her ("of thee") and in the divine power, and no man is named.

[L3] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." [L2] עַלְמָה (almah, H5959) means a young woman of marriageable age. It is the word used in Genesis 24:43 for the girl who "cometh forth to draw water." Matthew applies the verse to this birth in Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son," and there the Greek is parthenos (G3933). [L4] The Isaiah sign and Matthew's use of it agree with Mary's own words in Luke 1:34. The sign was that a virgin would conceive.

## 4. Joseph is called father only as a reputed or legal father

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." [L2] The word is ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, G3543 nomizō), meaning "to think, to hold by custom or opinion." Luke himself marks the relation as an opinion.

[L3] Matthew 1:20 shows Joseph called "son of David," and he is the legal link to David's house. Matthew 1:25 shows that he named the child, which is a father's legal act: "and he called his name JESUS."

**Anticipating the opponent's likely witnesses.**

[L1] John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" [L4] These are the words of unbelieving hearers, reporting what they supposed. Luke 3:23 uses the same reputed sense with "as was supposed." Also, in the same verse they object to what he says of himself: "I came down from heaven."

[L1] Luke 2:48: "behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." [L3] The answer comes in the next verse, Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" The child corrects the title. The word "father" here fits the household sense, and the child names another Father. [L2] "Father" is πατήρ (patēr, G3962), which can mean the legal or household head as well as the begetter. Which sense applies has to be decided by the context, and Luke 1:34-35 and 3:23 give that context.

## 5. Mary's flesh and the body prepared

[L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law." [L2] "Made" is γενόμενον (genomenon, G1096 ginomai), meaning "to come to be." Paul names the woman as the only human parent, and he names no man.

[L3] Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me." [L2] The word is κατηρτίσω (katērtisō, G2675 katartizō), meaning "to fit out, to prepare." The body is the Father's preparation and not the product of a man's seed.

[L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed." [L2] "Seed" is זֶרַע (zera, H2233). The text speaks of the woman's seed, not a man's seed.

[L3] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." [L4] This is the human descent. Combined with Luke 1:35 ("born of thee") it places the Davidic descent through Mary and not through a male begetter.

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew's genealogy breaks the begetting at Joseph: it changes from "begat" (ἐγέννησεν, G1080) in Matthew 1:2 to "the husband of Mary, of whom (ἧς, feminine) was born Jesus" in Matthew 1:16, and Matthew 1:18 confirms it with "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost as its source: Matthew 1:20 "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost," with ἐκ (G1537, "out of"), and Matthew 1:18 "before they came together" with Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till she had brought forth," ginōskō (G1097).
3. Mary and the angel state the same thing: Luke 1:34 "seeing I know not a man" with ginōskō (G1097), and Luke 1:35 "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee," with dio (G1352, "for which reason") and Isaiah 7:14 "a virgin shall conceive" (H5959) as cited in Matthew 1:23.
4. Joseph's fatherhood is reputed and legal only: Luke 3:23 "as was supposed" with ἐνομίζετο (G3543), and Luke 2:48-49 where the child answers "thy father" with "my Father's business" (πατήρ, G3962).
5. Therefore Christ had no human biological father: Galatians 4:4 "made of a woman" (G1096) and Hebrews 10:5 "a body hast thou prepared me" (G2675) carry the conclusion with links 1 to 4. He was conceived of the Holy Ghost in Mary, and Joseph was his husband-of-Mary guardian and legal father.

CHALLENGER (record's reading) -- ROUND 1, CHALLENGE

# Challenge: the seed of David out of a man's loins, and Joseph named father

The defender's chain asks one passive verb, one preposition and one tense to outweigh the promise that fixes where the seed comes from. I take each link by number and then aim at the keystone, D5.

## The ground the chain must fit: the seed comes out of a man's body

[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom." The promised seed comes out of David's own body.

[L3] Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne." Peter applies that oath to Christ: out of David's loins, according to the flesh.

[L3] Hebrews 7:14: "it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda." [L3] The same writer uses the loins as the channel of descent: "he was yet in the loins of his father" (Hebrews 7:10).

[L2] ὀσφύς (osphys, "loins") stands in Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:10. It names the man's body as the source of offspring.

[L3] Numbers 1:2: "by the house of their fathers, with the number of their names, every male by their polls." Tribe and house are reckoned through the father.

[L4] Footed on 2 Samuel 7:12 and Acts 2:30 [L1, L3] and on osphys [L2], the promised seed proceeds out of a man's loins. Any link that routes the flesh around a man must fit these rows. The defender's chain does not show that fit.

**Question to the defender:** according to Hebrews 7:14, how is it "evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda," given the law of Numbers 1:2 and 1:18, "by the house of their fathers"?

## LINK D1: Matthew 1:16

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] The noun is ἀνήρ (anēr, "husband, man"). The verb is ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born"), the passive of gennaō ("to beget, to bear"), used with ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom," feminine). This passive names the bearing, which is the mother's act. Matthew uses the same act in Matthew 1:21: "she shall bring forth a son."

[L3] Matthew calls Joseph by the same word, anēr, three verses later: "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19). The angel addresses him as the Davidic heir: "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20). The canon's way for a husband to beget is by knowing his wife: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1).

[L4] Footed on Matthew 1:16 and 1:19 [L1, L3] and on anēr and egennēthē [L2], the verse does three things:
- it keeps Joseph inside the Davidic line;
- it names him husband, the man who begets by knowing his wife (Genesis 4:1);
- it puts the bearing on the mother.

The feminine pronoun marks who bore the child. It does not remove the husband. The defender's claim that the grammar "deliberately cuts Joseph out as the begetter" is an inference with one footing, the pronoun, and it passes over Matthew 1:19 and 1:20.

## LINK D2: "of the Holy Ghost," "before they came together," "till"

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The KJV margin on "conceived" reads "Gr. begotten."

[L2] ἐκ (ek, "out of, from") with God or the Spirit names an origin in God. Those said to be born of God in this way also have human parents.

[L3] John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." 1 John 5:1: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God." Every believer described there had a father and a mother. "Of God" with ek states where the life is claimed from. It does not state who the man was.

[L3] The angel's "for" (γάρ, gar, "for, because") gives the reason for the command "take unto thee Mary thy wife." The child is the seed God claims as his own: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14). That claim was first spoken of Solomon, who had a begetting father: "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father" (1 Chronicles 28:6). Both fathers appear in one verse.

On the timing rows, quoted as written:
- [L1] "before they came together, she was found with child" (Matthew 1:18). This dates the finding.
- [L3] Matthew sets what "came together" means by what follows: "took unto him his wife" (Matthew 1:24), that is, bringing her into his house.
- [L3] The law names that same step: a man "that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her" (Deuteronomy 20:7).
- [L3] The law calls the betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24).
- [L1] "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25). The "till" bounds the abstinence to the pregnancy after the taking.

[L4] Footed on Matthew 1:19-20 and 1:24-25 [L1], Deuteronomy 20:7 and 22:24 [L3], and gar and ek [L2]: Joseph and Mary were husband and wife from the espousal, and Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal. The child is of his loins, which is what Acts 2:30 requires. The defender's sentence "So no human male begot the child" rests on reading ek as begetter. John 1:13 and 1 Chronicles 28:6 show that ek and "my son" do not carry that reading.

## LINK D3: Luke 1:34-35 and Isaiah 7:14

[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

[L2] ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "I do not know a man") is a present active indicative. It states her condition at the moment the angel spoke. The promise she is answering is future tense: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb" (Luke 1:31), συλλήψῃ (syllēmpsē, "thou shalt conceive").

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."

[L2] The first verb is ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai), from eperchomai ("to come upon"). The second is ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei), from episkiazō ("to overshadow").

[L3] A father's declaration also enrolled a child into a tribe: Genesis 48:5, "Ephraim and Manasseh... are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine." [L2] ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") is active and runs unbroken through the list, as in Matthew 1:2. Verse 16 turns to the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") with ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom," feminine singular).

### 1. What Held at L1-L2-L3?

A point appears here only if no charge in either side's lists contests it. Every point subject to a charge or press is set under Section 2 with both sides' answers, unresolved.

- **The grammatical form of Matthew 1:16:** In Matthew 1:16, the verb ἐγεννήθη (*egennēthē*, G1080) is passive ("was born"), the relative pronoun ἧς (*hēs*) is feminine singular ("of whom"), pointing to Mary, and Joseph is termed ἀνήρ (*anēr*, G435, "husband").
- **The wording of Matthew 1:18, 1:20, and 1:25:** The text states: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:18); "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20); and "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS" (Matthew 1:25).
- **The text of 2 Samuel 7:12 and Acts 2:30:** The promise states: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12), and Peter cites the oath: "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30), with ὀσφύς (*osphys*, G3751, "loins").
- **Joseph's Davidic lineage in the text:** Luke 1:27 states "a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David"; Luke 2:4 states "he was of the house and lineage of David"; and Matthew 1:20 records the address "Joseph, thou son of David."
- **Mary's address to the twelve-year-old child:** Luke 2:48 records: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
- **The Hebrew and Greek terms in the prophetic sign:** In Isaiah 7:14 the Hebrew text reads עַלְמָה (*almah*, H5959, "young woman"), and Matthew 1:23 applies the quotation using παρθένος (*parthenos*, G3933, "a virgin").
- **The wording of Galatians 4:4 and Romans 1:3:** Paul writes: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law" (Galatians 4:4), and "Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3), both employing the participle of γίνομαι (*ginomai*, G1096) with the preposition ἐκ (*ek*, G1537).

# CLOSE ROUND: the defender's final defense of D1 to D5

I do not add links or renumber. Every verse is quoted exactly from the KJV.

---

## D1: the genealogy breaks at Joseph

**Footing held.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;"
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] gennaō (G1080) is "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)". In Matthew 1:2 it is active, with the father as subject.
- [L2] In Matthew 1:16 the verb is passive, "was born", and the relative "of whom" (hēs) is feminine. The verb of begetting is not attached to Joseph.
- [L2] Joseph is called anēr (G435), "husband", of Mary. He is not called the one who begat.
- [L4] The active "begat" runs through every name until Joseph. At Joseph it is replaced by a passive verb tied to Mary. So the genealogy's own grammar breaks the begetting at Joseph.

**C1 (seed through fathers).** The challenger's footing is Hebrews 7:10, Romans 1:3 and Numbers 1:18.
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."
- [L4] This shows how seed runs between fathers and sons. It does not say Jesus was begotten that way.
- [L1] Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh;"
- [L2] The verb is ginomai (G1096), "made" or "come to be". It is not gennaō, "beget". Paul says "made", and nothing in the verse names a begetter.
- [L3] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman". The same verb is used there, with the woman as the source.
- [L4] Paul puts "made of the seed of David" beside "made of a woman" without a begetter, so the descent in Romans 1:3 is carried through the woman. That fits D1.

**ANSWER: Genesis 3:15 -- D1 --** "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."
- [L2] The word "seed" is set with a woman: "her seed". No father is named in the verse.
- [L3] Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee". The bearing is from the woman, and Luke 1:35 names no begetter other than the Holy Ghost.
- [L4] So Scripture does speak of seed from the woman without a father at the head. That agrees with D1's break at Joseph.

**ANSWER: Genesis 48:5 -- D1 --** "And now thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, which were born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt, [are] mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine."
- [L2] bên (H1121) includes "grandson". Jacob's claim on the two sons is by adoption: "[are] mine".
- [L4] Adoption takes a descendant into a house. It is a legal claim, and this is the category of D4 and D5: Joseph's relation to Jesus is legal, with Mary as the child's mother.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:15 -- D1 --** "And Eliud begat Eleazar; and Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob;"
- [L2] The verb is gennaō, active, in each clause.
- [L3] Matthew 1:16 then changes the verb.
- [L4] The contrast between the unbroken active line of Matthew 1:15 and the passive of Matthew 1:16 is the break that D1 states.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:16 -- D1 --** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] Matthew 1:16 uses "was born" (gennaō, passive) and the feminine "of whom".
- [L3] Matthew 1:21: "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS". She brings forth, and Joseph names.
- [L4] Matthew assigns the bearing to Mary and the naming to Joseph. That is the division between mother and legal father.

---

## D2: the conception is of the Holy Ghost

**Footing held.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The margin reads "conceived: Gr. begotten."
- [L2] The verb is gennaō (G1080), the same verb as in the genealogy, with the Holy Ghost (pneuma hagios, G4151, G40) as source.
- [L4] Matthew 1:18 dates the finding before the coming together. Matthew 1:20 names the begetting source as the Holy Ghost. The genealogy's begetting-verb is thereby attributed to the Holy Ghost, and no human begetter is given.

**C2 (the challenger says Matthew 1:19 supplies two grounds only).**
- [L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- [L2] apolyō (G630) includes "divorce". Joseph's purpose is to dissolve a bond because of what is found in her.
- [L3] Matthew 1:18 gives the time of that finding: "before they came together".
- [L3] Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife". The angel meets Joseph's fear with the origin of the child.
- [L2] phobeō (G5399) is "to frighten ... to be alarmed". The angel answers a fear.
- [L4] I withdraw the bare sentence "he knew the child was not his" as a quoted statement of Matthew. What stands is narrower and has its footing. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding before they came together. Matthew 1:19 shows a purpose to divorce. Matthew 1:20 meets his fear with "of the Holy Ghost". Together these show the pregnancy preceded union and that Joseph needed the angel's word.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:25 -- D2 --** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."
- [L2] ginōskō (G1097) is "to know", and in marriage it is the idiom of union.
- [L3] Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain". There the knowing precedes the conception. In Matthew 1:25 the "knew her not" runs until she had brought forth.
- [L4] So Matthew states the order, with no knowing before the birth. That is consistent with D2.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:18 -- D2 --** "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] heurisko (found) is the discovery-word.
- [L3] Matthew 1:24: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife".
- [L4] Matthew places the coming together after the finding, at the taking of Matthew 1:24, so it is not within the espousal.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:20 -- D2 --** "But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] The "for" gives the reason for the command "fear not". The reason is the source of the child, the Holy Ghost.
- [L3] John 1:13 and 1 John 5:1 use "of God" for believers' birth. Believers are born "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God". So "of God" is set against the man's will in the verse itself, and the challenger's use of John 1:13 does not help him.
- [L4] The angel's reason for taking her is the divine source of the child. That is how D2 reads the verse.

**ANSWER: Deuteronomy 20:7 -- D2 --** "And what man [is there] that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? let him go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man take her."
- [L2] The law's phrase is "betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her". Betrothal and taking are distinct.
- [L2] In Matthew 1:20 the angel's "take" is paralambanō (G3880), "receive near ... associate with oneself in any familiar or intimate act or relation".
- [L3] Matthew 1:24: "took unto him his wife".
- [L4] Joseph is betrothed but has not yet taken her. This is the law's own distinction, and it fits "before they came together".

**ANSWER: Deuteronomy 22:24 -- D2 --** "...the man, because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife".
- [L2] The law's word for a betrothed woman is "wife" (H802). The law is not speaking of the union.
- [L3] Matthew 1:18 speaks of "before they came together", so Matthew uses "wife" in the same legal sense as the law.
- [L4] Matthew's "wife" for the espoused fits the law's use. It does not show that they had come together.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:31 -- D2 --** "And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS."
- [L1] The verse is the angel's announcement of a conception still to come.
- [L3] Luke 1:35 gives its means: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee".
- [L4] The future conception and the Holy Ghost's coming are linked in the same speech.

---

## D3: Mary and the angel say the same

**Footing held.**
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Here ginōskō (G1097) is "to know" in the marital sense.
- [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] dio (G1352), "for which reason", ties the title to the Holy Ghost's coming.
- [L3] Matthew 1:23 cites Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child".
- [L4] Mary's question arises from the very condition of "I know not a man". The angel's answer gives the Holy Ghost as the means, not Joseph.

**C4 (the angel's pattern is Elisabeth with her husband).**
- [L1] Luke 1:36: "And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren."
- [L3] Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
- [L4] The sign of Elisabeth is that God overcomes barrenness. It answers Mary's doubt about whether the thing is possible. Mary's question in Luke 1:34 is how, because she knows not a man. The angel's reply does not point to Joseph. It points to "the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee".
- [L4] The "also" (kai) sets two conceptions side by side. It does not make them identical in kind. The angel says the second is by the Holy Ghost.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:13 -- D3 --** "But the angel said unto him, Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John."
- [L2] "Bear thee" names Zacharias as the father.
- [L3] Luke 1:31 says to Mary only "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son". Luke 1:35 gives the Holy Ghost, not the husband.
- [L4] The two announcements differ in the very phrase. For Elisabeth, the angel says "bear thee". For Mary, there is no "bear thee", and the answer is "the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee".

**ANSWER: Luke 1:35 -- D3 --** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] dio (G1352), "for which reason", links the Holy Ghost's coming to the title.
- [L3] Luke 1:32 gives the Davidic title and throne: "shall be called the Son of the Highest". Luke 1:35 gives the ground of the title, which is the Holy Ghost's coming.
- [L4] In Luke 1:35 the angel's reason for the title is the Holy Ghost. I read D3's "therefore" as the angel's own link.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:27 -- D3 --** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name [was] Mary."
- [L2] parthenos (virgin) is used of Mary twice in the verse, and she is espoused.
- [L3] Luke 1:34 shows her state at the angel's word: "I know not a man".
- [L4] Luke 1:27 names Joseph as the man of the espousal. Luke 1:34 shows she had not come together with him. The two verses fit.

- [L1] The sign is given by "the Lord himself".
- [L2] The word is almah (H5959). Matthew 1:23 renders it with parthenos (G3933, virgin).

- [L2] The sign is of the LORD's own choosing, whether "in the depth, or in the height above".
- [L3] Isaiah 7:14: "the Lord himself shall give you a sign".
- [L4] The sign is the Lord's own gift, and Matthew 1:22 reads it as fulfilled in this birth.

**ANSWER: Genesis 24:16 -- D3 --** "And the damsel [was] very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her".
- [L2] bᵉthûwlâh (H1330) is a virgin, with the clause "neither had any man known her".
- [L3] Genesis 24:43 applies almah (H5959) to the same girl.

## D4: Joseph's fatherhood is reputed and legal

**Footing held.**
- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".
- [L2] The word is nomizō, "to suppose", from the same family as nomos, "law, custom".
- [L1] Luke 2:49: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
- [L2] patēr (G3962), "father", is used here of another than Joseph.
- [L3] Matthew 1:21 and 1:25: Joseph "shalt call his name JESUS" and "he called his name JESUS".
- [L4] Jesus is the son of Joseph as supposed, and by naming. Luke 2:49 gives a different father.

**C5 (one person can have a begetting father and "my son").**
- [L1] 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."
- [L2] bâchar (H977), "select", is the word for the choosing.
- [L3] 2 Samuel 12:24 states the act in the text: "David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in unto her, and lay with her".
- [L4] Solomon's two fatherhoods are each stated in a verse. For Jesus, Scripture states only the second: Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 give the Holy Ghost, and Luke 3:23 gives Joseph as only "supposed". So the Solomon case does not give Jesus a begetting father. It shows what a text says when there is one.

**ANSWER: Luke 3:23 -- D4 --** "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli,"
- [L2] The word is nomizō, "suppose".

**ANSWER: Luke 4:22 -- D4 --** "And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth. And they said, Is not this Joseph's son?"
- [L2] The speakers are "they", the hearers.
- [L3] John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?"

**ANSWER: Luke 2:48 and Luke 2:49 -- D4 --** "his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." And: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

---

## D5: Christ had no human biological father

**Footing held.**
- [L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,"
- [L2] ginomai (G1096) is "made", "come to be", with the woman as the source named.
- [L1] Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me".
- [L2] katartizō (G2675) is "to fit, prepare", with God as the one who prepares.
- [L4] Galatians 4:4 names a woman and no man. Hebrews 10:5 names God as preparing the body. Together with D1 to D4 these give the conclusion: the body was prepared by God in Mary, and Joseph is husband of Mary and legal father.

**C3 (the loins of David).** The challenger says Acts 2:30 carries David's loins through the Davidic man.

- [L3] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh". Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman".
- [L3] Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David".

The legal heir of David's house is the one Joseph names (Matthew 1:21, 1:25).

**ANSWER: Acts 2:30 -- D5 --** quoted above.
- [L2] osphys (loins) is the word of Hebrews 7:10 for the father's loins, and Acts 2:30 applies it to David, the ancestor.
- [L4] "Fruit of his loins" is descent from David, which can be generations on. 2 Samuel 7:12 says "I will set up thy seed after thee". The text does not say the descent runs through a living man's begetting in the last generation.

**ANSWER: 2 Samuel 7:12 -- D5 --** "And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom."

**ANSWER: Psalms 132:11 -- D5 --** quoted above.
- [L2] "I will set" is God's act. The word is "belly", from the margin.

# Round 4: the challenger's close

I add no witness and no premise. Each verse below was cited in my earlier rounds and is quoted from the KJV. My links keep the numbers my link round gave them.

**My answer to the subject:** yes. Christ had a biological father, Joseph, the husband of Mary, of the house of David. The seed promised to David came out of a man's loins, according to the flesh.   This is intent and its grounds. The angel's answer is the command to take her.

Deuteronomy 22:24 calls the betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife". "Of" (ek) is the covenant-origin form of John 1:13, "Which were born... of God," and 1 John 5:1, "is born of God."
- [L3] Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". This is the canon's stated means of begetting.
- [L4] Joseph and Mary were husband and wife from the espousal: "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19), "Mary thy wife" (Matthew 1:20), "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24). Seed out of a man's body requires knowing, as in Genesis 4:1. So, at [L4] on those rows, Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal.

  - Matthew 1:18, "before they came together, she was found with child," dates the finding.
  - Matthew 1:24, "took unto him his wife," is the taking. Deuteronomy 20:7 names that same step: "betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her".

## C4: the angel's sign to Mary is Elisabeth, who conceived of her husband; the angel's verbs are empowerment and presence

- [L1] Luke 1:36: "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age".

  - eperchomai (G1904), "come upon." It is the same verb as Acts 1:8, "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses," which is power given to the apostles.
  - episkiazō (G1982), "overshadow." It is the same verb as Luke 9:34, "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them," which is the cloud of presence.

- [L1] 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."

Luke 1:32 gives "the Son of the Highest" with "the throne of his father David." So the title is the covenant title of David's seed, and it stands beside a begetting father.

- [L1] Luke 2:48 is Mary's own word: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
- [L3] The other registers:
  - The narrator: "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27), "his parents" (Luke 2:41), and "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33).
  - A disciple: "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45).
  - The town: "Is not this Joseph's son?" (Luke 4:22).
- [L2] Luke 3:23, "(as was supposed)," uses enomizeto from nomizō (G3543), "to do by law (usage)... be wont." It is the same form as Acts 16:13, "where prayer was wont to be made." The reckoning goes "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:2).

- [L4] Mary, the narrator, a disciple and the town all name Joseph as father. Luke's verb is the verb of custom and law, and the law reckons a child by the father's house. "Made of a woman" is the common phrase for a man's mortal birth. So these witnesses agree with the seed rows.

---

## Final words

David's seed proceeds "out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12) and is "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3). The son of David named in the account is "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19), and Mary says to the child, "thy father and I" (Luke 2:48).

From the seed rows, the knowing of Genesis 4:1, the marriage from the espousal, and the "till" of Matthew 1:25, I hold at [L4] that Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal. The child is the fruit of David's loins through him. "Of the Holy Ghost" marks the child God claims as his own: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14).

Christ had a biological father, and the text names him: Joseph, of the house and lineage of David.

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position [L4].** The KJV says Jesus was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no man involved. Joseph was his legal and supposed father, not his begetter. By "biological father" I mean a male who begets the child by natural generation. I make no claim about anything beyond the text.

## 1. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost," and no man is named

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** The phrase is *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537, G4151, G40), "out of the Spirit, holy." The preposition *ek* marks source or origin. The verse names the origin of the pregnancy, and the origin is not a man.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** The verb is *gennēthen* (G1080, *gennaō*), "begotten or conceived." The same word is used of fathers begetting in Matthew 1:2–16. In Matthew 1:20 it is applied to what is "in her," with the Holy Ghost as source.
- **[L3]** John 4:24: "God is a Spirit." The source named in Matthew 1:20 is therefore not a male body, so the begetting is not biological in the ordinary sense.
- **[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the source of the conception as the Holy Ghost. John 4:24 says that source is spirit, not flesh. Together they show the conception did not come from a male human parent.

## 2. Matthew's genealogy breaks its own pattern at verse 16

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L2]** Verses 2–15 repeat *egennēsen* (G1080), "begat," with a male subject. Verse 16 changes to *egennēthē*, "was born," a passive form. The relative pronoun *hēs* (G3739) is feminine singular, "of whom [her]." The birth is traced to Mary alone, and Joseph is called only "the husband of Mary."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." This is the pattern the genealogy sets, and verse 16 departs from it at the last link.
- **[L4]** The chain of "begat" ends at Joseph. Jesus is not said to be begotten by him. He is "born" of Mary, who is named as the sole parent.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and says so

- **[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph… and the virgin's name was Mary."
- **[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933), "virgin."
- **[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- **[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097), "to know," used here of sexual knowledge, with *anēr* (G435), "a man, a male."
- **[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L2]** *dio kai*, "wherefore also," makes the cause explicit. The child is called Son of God because of the Holy Ghost's coming. A male parent is not named.
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." Joseph's *ginōskō* is withheld until the birth.
- **[L4]** Mary's question in Luke 1:34 is answered by the Holy Ghost's coming in 1:35, with no mention of any man. Matthew 1:25 confirms Joseph had no part before the birth.

## 4. The prophecies point the same way

- **[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."
- **[L2]** *almah* (H5959) is the Hebrew word the KJV renders "virgin." *Harah* (H2029), "conceive," is the verb of the sign, and the sign is the conception itself.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son… Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."
- **[L3]** Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head." The promised deliverer is called "her seed" (*zera*, H2233, "seed"), the woman's seed and not the man's.
- **[L3]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." The verb *genomenon* (G1096) means "made, become," and the source named is *ek gynaikos* (G1135, "out of a woman"), not a man.
- **[L4]** Genesis 3:15 names the woman's seed, Isaiah 7:14 gives a virgin conceiving, and Galatians 4:4 names only "a woman." Together these form one line of text that names no human male source.

## 5. Joseph is the supposed father only

- **[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- **[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543, *nomizō*), "was thought, was reckoned." It marks opinion or legal reckoning as opposed to fact.
- **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "Thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Mary speaks of Joseph as "father."
- **[L3]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" The child corrects the title and points to a different Father.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19–20: Joseph is told to "take unto thee Mary thy wife." Taking and naming (Matthew 1:21, 25) are acts of adoption and legal fatherhood.
- **[L4]** Luke 3:23 marks Joseph's fatherhood as supposed. Luke 2:49 names another Father. Matthew 1:20, 25 describe Joseph's role as taking and naming, not begetting. Joseph is legal father only.

## 6. The royal line gives a further reason

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:11–12: "Josias begat Jechonias… And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel." Joseph is descended from Jechonias (Matthew 1:16).
- **[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30: "Write ye this man childless… for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
- **[L2]** *zera* (H2233), "seed," is the word here for physical descendants.
- **[L3]** Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." Luke 3:23–31 traces a separate line through Heli to David by way of Nathan (Luke 3:31).
- **[L4]** If Joseph, of Jechonias's seed, had begotten Jesus, Jeremiah 22:30 would bar the throne of David that Luke 1:32 promises. Matthew gives the legal line through Joseph. The promise is kept through Mary's line, and Jesus is of David "according to the flesh" through her (Romans 1:3).

## Anticipated press: John 6:42 and Luke 2:48

- **[L1]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"
- **[L4]** This is the crowd speaking, not the narrator. It matches the "as was supposed" of Luke 3:23, which is the narrator's own marking of what the people thought. The word *enomizeto* (G3543) stands behind that marking and keeps the verses consistent.

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. The conception was "of the Holy Ghost" with no man named as source. Footing: Matthew 1:18, 1:20 [L1]; *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Spirit, holy," and *gennaō*, "begotten" [L2]; John 4:24, "God is a Spirit" [L3].
2. Matthew's genealogy ends the line of "begat" at Joseph and traces the birth of Jesus to Mary alone. Footing: Matthew 1:16 [L1]; feminine *hēs*, "of whom [her]," and *egennēthē*, "was born," against *egennēsen*, "begat" [L2]; Matthew 1:2 [L3].
3. Mary was a virgin who "knew not a man," and the Holy Ghost's coming is the stated cause. Footing: Luke 1:34–35 [L1]; *parthenos*, "virgin," and *ginōskō*, "to know" [L2]; Matthew 1:25 [L3].
4. The prophecies name the woman's seed and a virgin conceiving, not a man's. Footing: Isaiah 7:14 [L1]; *almah* (the Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin") and *zera*, "seed" [L2]; Genesis 3:15 and Galatians 4:4 [L3].
5. Joseph is father by legal reckoning only. Footing: Luke 3:23, "as was supposed" [L1]; *enomizeto*, "was thought, reckoned" [L2]; Luke 2:49 [L3].
6. Christ had no biological father.
 Footing: links 1–5, resting on Matthew 1:18, 1:20 [L1], *ek pneumatos hagiou* [L2], and Luke 1:35 [L3].

- **[L4]** Matthew 1:18 dates the finding. It falls while Mary "was espoused," before the taking of 1:24. Matthew 1:25 then reads "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son," and covers the time after the taking until the birth.

So the order is: the espousal, the finding, the taking, then abstinence until the birth. The defender's own Luke 2:5 calls her "Mary his espoused wife, being great with child." That is the espousal C4 names. Within it, Joseph is "her husband" (Matthew 1:19), Mary is "thy wife" (Matthew 1:20), and the law calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24).

- **[L4]** The text's stated means of conceiving is the husband knowing his wife: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1). The seed rows require "the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30). So, footed on these rows, Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins.

**Matthew 1:19.**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L2]** *thelō* (G2309), "to determine… choose." The verse states an intent, "was minded," and gives its two grounds: just, and not willing to make her a public example.
- **[L3]** The angel answers that thought with a ground for taking her. Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The "for" points to the seed God claims as his own. 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."
- **[L4]** The verse gives the grounds of Joseph's intent. The angel's "for" grounds the taking in God's covenant claim on David's seed. That fits a husband and his wife.

## 3. The defender's "split" charge answered: Romans 1:3–4 names both sides

The defender wrote that the challenger "must split the one object into a spirit part from God and a flesh part from Joseph."

- **[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- **[L3]** Romans 1:4: "And declared [to be] the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead: [declared: Gr. determined]."
- **[L2]** At Romans 1:3, the seed-word is *sperma* (G4690). Its lexicon gloss reads: "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm')." It stands with *sarx* (G4561), "flesh."
- **[L4]** Paul himself sets "according to the flesh" beside "according to the spirit of holiness." The flesh is David's seed. The Sonship is "declared" by the resurrection. John 3:6 keeps the same two kinds: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."

The defender points out that Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 share the verb *ginomai* (G1096). Its gloss reads "used with great latitude." What sets Romans 1:3 apart is its seed-word. Galatians 4:4's "made of a woman" is the phrase the defender granted is said of sons with fathers (Job 14:1).

## 4. "His father David," the angel's words, and the voices

**Luke 1:32.** Luke 1:32 gives "the throne of his father David." The same chapter gives the house of David to Joseph: "a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David" (Luke 1:27). Luke 2:4 says the same: "he was of the house and lineage of David." The throne promised to Mary is the throne of the house she was espoused into.

**The angel's words to Joseph.** The angel who says "the young child and his mother" (Matthew 2:13) also says "Joseph, thou son of David… thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Matthew 1:20–21). That is the act the angel gave to Zacharias, a father: "thou shalt call his name John" (Luke 1:13).

**The narrator and Mary.** Luke's own narration says "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27). It is the same narrator who writes 3:23. Mary, who heard the angel, says "thy father and I" (Luke 2:48). After "my Father's business," the narrator writes: "he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them" (Luke 2:51).

**"Supposed."** The defender's "supposing" rows are active verbs of men's guesses (Luke 2:44; Acts 14:19; Acts 21:29). Luke 3:23 has the passive *enomizeto*. That is the form of Acts 16:13, "where prayer was wont to be made." Its lexicon gloss is "properly, to do by law (usage)." It names a reckoning by usage, the reckoning "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:18).

**The two genealogies.** I hold both registers as the text gives them, and I add no construct. Each runs to Joseph and then to his father. Luke 3:23 reads "the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli." Matthew 1:16 reads "Jacob begat Joseph." Each is a father's house.

### 1. Held at L1–L2–L3 (Uncontested Ground)

The following points were established with lower-layer citations and remained uncontested by either side across all rounds:

- **Joseph's Davidic Lineage:** The text explicitly identifies Joseph as belonging to the house and lineage of David: Luke 1:27 states, "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary"; Luke 2:4 states, "And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:)". Both sides quote these verses and agree that the text directly assigns the house of David to Joseph.
- **Absence of Stated Tribal Identification for Mary:** The canonical text nowhere explicitly states the tribal lineage or pedigree of Mary. The defender conceded across Rounds 2, 3, and 4: "the KJV does not state Mary's tribe in so many words." The challenger noted and accepted this concession.
- **Natural Generation in Corroborative Witnesses:** The phrases "another seed" in Genesis 4:25 ("For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel") and "born of a woman" in Job 14:1 ("Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble") occur in contexts describing individuals who had human fathers. The defender explicitly granted this in Round 2, Round 3, and Round 4.
- **The Textual Construction of Matthew 1:16:** Matthew 1:16 reads: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." Both sides agree that through verses 2–15 the genealogy utilizes the active verb *egennēsen* ("begat") with male subjects, whereas verse 16 employs the passive verb *egennēthē* ("was born") with the feminine singular relative pronoun *hēs* ("of whom").
- **Divergence of the Genealogies Without Narrated Resolution:** Matthew 1:12 ("Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel") and Luke 3:27 ("which was the son of Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri") present different ancestral lines that the canonical text leaves without an explicit reconciling narrative. Both sides agreed to hold both rows as written without importing external constructs.

---

### 2. Concessions, Narrowings, and Link Status

  - *Premise:* The conception was "of the Holy Ghost" with no man named as source.
