  3. "Till" (G2193) bounds the not-knowing to the pregnancy after the taking (Matthew 1:25). The defender conceded in close that this verse does not prove Joseph never knew her before.
  4. Joseph and Mary were husband and wife from the espousal: "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19), "Mary thy wife" (Matthew 1:20, G1135), and the law's "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24). Matthew 1:19 states intent (G1014) and two grounds, and no verb of knowledge.
  5. Luke 1:34's "I know not a man" is present tense, her state when the angel spoke.
  6. The canon's stated means of conception is the husband knowing his wife (Genesis 4:1).

  From these rows, with the seed rows of C1, the chain stands: Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins.

## C6: KEPT. The conclusion: Christ had a biological father, Joseph

- [L1] Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh;"
- [L2] Sárx (G4561) means flesh, "the body ... or as the means of kindred." Almah (H5959) in Isaiah 7:14 means a young woman. It is not bethulah, the virgin-word.
- [L3] Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS." Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Luke 1:62: "they made signs to his father, how he would have him called." Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." Isaiah 7:16: "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings." Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman." Job 14:1: "Man [that is] born of a woman [is] of few days." Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."
- [L4] Each row adds a line to the same chain:
  - The flesh is "the means of kindred" (G4561), and it is David's seed (Romans 1:3) out of loins (C1).
  - The naming is the father's act. The angel tells Joseph "thou shalt call" (Matthew 1:21), as the angel tells Zacharias (Luke 1:13), and the father is asked the name (Luke 1:62).
  - Matthew 1:16's "was born" narrates the birth by the mother. It does not say no man begat.
  - "Made of a woman" is said of men who had fathers (Job 14:1; Matthew 11:11). The defender conceded that Galatians 4:4 does not exclude a father.
  - Isaiah's sign is a young woman's (H5959), bounded by its own days (Isaiah 7:16).

Precept upon precept, line upon line, the text gives one answer. The seed is David's according to the flesh, out of loins. The father is Joseph, named by Mary, the town, a disciple and the narrator. The house is Joseph's. The Holy Ghost's coming is presence and power. The title is the covenant son's. Joseph knew Mary his wife, and the child is his son. Christ had a biological father, and his name was Joseph.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** "Biological father" means the male who, by his seed, caused the conception. On the KJV text, Christ was conceived of Mary by the Holy Ghost, and no man begat him. Joseph was his legal and reputed father only.

---

## 1. Mary was a virgin when she conceived

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."
**[L2]** The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), "a virgin," a woman who has not had sexual relations. Luke applies it to Mary twice in this one verse.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
**[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097), "to know," is the verb for sexual knowledge. *andra* (from *anēr*, G435) is "a man." Mary's question is how conception could happen when she has had no relations with any man. Her words rule out a male source before the angel answers.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." Matthew cites this as fulfilled in Mary.
**[L3]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."
**[L2]** The Hebrew is *ha'almah* (H5959), "the young woman." The KJV renders the same word "virgin" in Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water." Genesis 24:16 describes that same woman as one "neither had any man known her." Matthew's Greek *parthenos* (G3933) settles the sense for the fulfilment.

**[L4]** The prophecy named a virgin, and Luke 1:27 and 1:34 supply her. *Parthenos* (a virgin) and *ginōskō* (know) in Luke 1:34, together with Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in Matthew 1:23, show that the conception occurred with no man involved.

---

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost, not a man

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Ghost," uses *ek* (G1537), a preposition of source or origin. The text also says "before they came together" (*prin ē synelthein*, G4160), so the pregnancy predates any union with Joseph.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** *gennēthen* (G1080, *gennaō*) is "begotten" or "conceived." It is the same root as the "begat" of the genealogy. Where the genealogy names a man as the one who begat, this verse gives *ek pneumatos hagiou* as the source.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L2]** *episkiazō* (G1982), "to overshadow," means to cover with a shadow. It describes divine power at work, not a man's act. *dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the title Son of God follow from this manner of conception.

**[L3]** Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." The angel offers this as the answer to Mary's question about how, with no man, she could conceive.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 give the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*). Luke 1:35 gives the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as the agency, and Luke 1:34 has already excluded a man. The text names one source, and it is not a man.

---

## 3. Matthew's genealogy breaks its "begat" pattern at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
**[L2]** *egennēsen* (G1080), "begat," has a male subject in every earlier link. *anēr* (G435) is "husband." The phrase *ex hēs* ("of whom") is feminine singular, so the one born came out of Mary, not out of Joseph. The verb also changes: the passive *egennēthē* ("was born") replaces "begat."
**[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren." This is the pattern of the whole list, and verse 16 departs from it.

**[L4]** Verses 2 to 15 follow the pattern "A begat B." Verse 16 stops the pattern at Joseph and uses the feminine "of whom" for Jesus. It calls Joseph "husband of Mary," not the one who begat Jesus. The grammar (G1080, passive; *ex hēs*, feminine) and the pattern of verse 2 show that Matthew deliberately withholds "begat" from Joseph.

---

## 4. Joseph is father only by supposition and by legal naming

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
**[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543), "was supposed" or "was reckoned," marks an opinion held by others, not a fact.

**[L1]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" This is the crowd's assumption.
**[L3]** Luke 2:48 and 2:49. Mary says, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing," and the child answers, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Mary speaks of Joseph as father in the household sense. The child then points to a different Father.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."
**[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097) is again "know," the same verb as in Luke 1:34. Joseph did not know Mary until after the birth.
**[L3]** Matthew 1:19, 1:20 and 1:21. Joseph, "being a just man," was "minded to put her away privily." The angel told him to "take unto thee Mary thy wife" and said "thou shalt call his name JESUS." Joseph acted on the angel's word and named the child as his own, which is a legal act. Matthew 1:19 shows he knew the child was not his, because he intended to put her away.

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 (*enomizeto*) and Matthew 1:25 (*ginōskō*) show that Joseph's fatherhood rested on opinion and law. Matthew 1:19 and 1:20 show he did not believe himself the father until the angel spoke. Luke 2:49 shows the child himself placed his true parentage elsewhere.

---

## 5. Further confirmation: "made of a woman" and "her seed"

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
**[L2]** *genomenon ek gynaikos* (G1096, G1537, G1135) is "become out of a woman." Paul names only the woman as the source.
**[L3]** Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed." **[L2]** *zera'* (H2233), "seed," is ordinarily the man's seed. Here it is called the woman's.
**[L3]** Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me." **[L2]** *katartizō* (G2675), "to fit" or "prepare," points to a body provided by God.

**[L4]** Galatians 4:4 and Genesis 3:15 agree with the Gospel narratives. The Son came by a woman, with no man named as his source.

---

## 6. The objection from the throne of David

**[L1]** Matthew 1:12: "Jechonias begat Salathiel." Joseph's line runs through Jechonias.
**[L3]** Jeremiah 22:30: "Write ye this man childless... for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
**[L3]** Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

**[L4]** Jeremiah 22:30 says no one from the seed of Jechonias would prosper on David's throne. Luke 1:32 and Romans 1:3 say Christ would hold that throne and be of David's seed. A man begotten by Joseph, who descended from Jechonias (Matthew 1:12), would be under that bar. The Davidic claim therefore agrees with a conception that did not come by Joseph's seed. It came through Mary (Luke 1:27, "of the house of David" in the same sentence as Joseph) and through legal naming by Joseph.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. Mary was a virgin who had not known a man when she conceived. Luke 1:27 ("a virgin"; *parthenos*, G3933) and Luke 1:34 ("I know not a man"; *ginōskō*, G1097); fulfilled prophecy in Isaiah 7:14 (*ha'almah*, H5959) and Matthew 1:23.
2. The source of the conception is stated as the Holy Ghost, not a man. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Ghost"; *gennēthen*, G1080), with Luke 1:35 ("the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee"; *episkiazō*, G1982).
3. Matthew 1:16 withholds "begat" from Joseph and says Jesus was born "of whom," feminine, meaning Mary. The footing is *egennēsen* (G1080) and the feminine *ex hēs* in Matthew 1:16, against the pattern in Matthew 1:2.
4. Joseph is father only by supposition and by legal naming. Luke 3:23 ("as was supposed"; *enomizeto*, G3543), Matthew 1:25 ("knew her not"; *ginōskō*, G1097), and Matthew 1:19-21 (Joseph intends to put her away, then takes her and names the child).
5. Therefore Christ had no biological father. Joseph was reputed and legal father, and the conception was of the Holy Ghost in a virgin (Matthew 1:18, 1:20, 1:23; Luke 1:34-35; Galatians 4:4, *genomenon ek gynaikos*, "become out of a woman").

# Challenge: the record names a father, and the seed is David's by the flesh

**Position.** The defender's keystone, D5 ("Therefore Christ had no biological father"), rests on four links. Each one reads a verse past its own words. Precept upon precept (Isaiah 28:10), the witnesses agree on four things. The promised seed comes out of a man's loins. The one man the text names is Joseph, of the house of David. The angel's verbs speak of power and presence, not begetting. The rows on timing describe a state at a set moment, not a permanent condition.

---

## MY DECLARED CHAIN

**C1. The promise requires seed out of a man's body, by the flesh.**

- [L2] The Hebrew is *mimme'eykha*, "out of thy bowels" (inward parts). This is a body word spoken to David, a man.

The defender's inferences below lack footing. The witnesses under each carry the layers.

6. **D4:** "Joseph's fatherhood rested on opinion and law."
   - Pressed with: Acts 16:13 (*enomizeto*); Luke 2:48; Luke 1:62-63.
7. **D5:** "Therefore Christ had no biological father."
   - Pressed with: 2 Samuel 7:12 (*mimme'eykha*); Acts 2:30 (*osphys*); Romans 1:3 (*kata sarka*); Hebrews 7:14 with Numbers 1:18 and Ezra 2:62.

rows.synthesis:
# SYNTHESIS

Scope note: chain-scoped debate (Isaiah 28:10). Both seats declared numbered chains and were pressed link-by-link; both link rounds exhibited footing; the challenger's close round pressed nothing new.

---

## 1. WHAT STOOD AT L1–L2–L3 (points no charge in either side's lists contests)

- **Luke 1:27** — "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary." The Davidic-house phrase attaches to Joseph. Defender: "The nearest antecedent of 'of the house of David' is Joseph." Challenger C2 builds on the same reading.
- **Luke 1:34 / 1:31 timing** — "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" is present indicative, her state when the angel spoke; "thou shalt conceive in thy womb" (Luke 1:31) is future. Defender: "I grant the present tense"; challenger: "Mary states her condition at the moment the angel spoke."
- **Matthew 1:18's verb** — "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." The verb is *synerchomai* (G4905), not G4160; it may name the taking of Matthew 1:24. Defender: "I wrongly gave G4160"; "I grant that *synerchomai* (G4905) may mean the taking."
- **Matthew 1:16** — "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." Passive *egennēthē* with feminine *ex hēs*; the verse names the mother and **does not state who begat**. Defender: "I agree the passive does not by itself state a begetter." Challenger: "The passive leaves the begetting unnarrated."
- **Matthew 1:25** — "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." *heōs hou* bounds the abstinence from the taking to the birth and does not reach back before the taking. Defender: "I grant that 'till' bounds the abstinence and does not itself reach back before the taking." Challenger: "Both sides now hold that limit."
- **Matthew 1:19** — "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." Two stated grounds and an intent; **no verb of knowing**. Defender: "They carry no verb of knowing, as the challenger says." Challenger: "No verb of knowledge stands in the row."
- **Genesis 4:1** — "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain." Both sides treat this as the canon's stated means of conceiving.
- **Matthew 1:20's *ek* with God** — "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost," margin "Gr. begotten" (*gennaō*, G1080). *Ek* with God is used of men who had fathers at John 1:13 ("but of God") and 1 John 5:1 ("is born of God"). Defender: "I grant that 'of God' is said of believers who had fathers."
- **Luke 1:35's verbs** — *eperchomai* (G1904) and *episkiazō* (G1982) also carry power/presence at Acts 1:8 ("after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you") and Luke 9:34 ("there came a cloud, and overshadowed them"). Defender: "I grant that *eperchomai* (G1904, 'come upon') and overshadowing alone do not mean begetting."
- **Luke 3:23's qualifier** — "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli." *nomizō* (G3543) in the same form names a true custom at Acts 16:13 ("where prayer was wont to be made"); the verb alone decides nothing. Both seats: defender "The verb alone does not decide"; challenger "The verb carries no verdict of its own."
- **Joseph carries two named fathers in the registers** — Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph" against Luke 3:23 "the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli." Both seats cite the divergence as the text's own data.
- **Two sonships in one verse at 1 Chronicles 28:6** — "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father." Both seats accept the L1 fact; only the inference from it differs.
- **Galatians 4:4's phrase is also used of men with fathers** — "made of a woman"; Job 14:1 "Man that is born of a woman is of few days"; Matthew 11:11 "Among them that are born of women." Defender conceded: "I withdraw them as decisive and keep them as confirming."
- **No KJV verse states Mary's Davidic descent** — Defender: "I admit that no KJV verse says so"; challenger: "The defender has granted that no verse states Mary's descent from David."

---

## 2. CONCESSIONS, NARROWINGS AND FOOTING — BOTH SIDES, BOTH LINK ROUNDS AND BOTH CLOSE ROUNDS

### DEFENDER's declared chain (D1–D5)

| Link | Status |
|---|---|
| **D1** (virgin, no man at conception) | **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE** — "I drop any reliance on *almah* (H5959) or Isaiah 7:14 alone." Kept on Luke 1:34–35, Matthew 1:18, 1:20, 1:23. |
| **D2** (Holy Ghost the stated source) | **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE** — "I drop the title argument." Kept on Matthew 1:20 with the margin "Gr. begotten" (*gennaō*). |
| **D3** (Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat") | **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE** — "LINK 3: NARROWED TO: the changed formula at Matthew 1:16, not the passive alone." |
| **D4** (supposition and legal naming) | **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE**, several limbs dropped: "My §6 claim that Luke 1:27 puts Mary in David's house floats free, and I withdraw it"; "I drop the reading of Matthew 1:25 and the naming verses as proof"; "I do not rest D4 on Jeremiah 22:30, and I withdraw it as a ground"; closing — "I have withdrawn Jeremiah 22:30, Ezra 2:61 and Matthew 1:25 as independent grounds." |
| **D5** (keystone: no biological father) | **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** on Matthew 1:18, 1:20 (margin *gennaō*), Luke 1:34–35, Matthew 1:16; presented in close as "the sum of D1 to D4." Two limbs inside it go to the challenger: "I grant the Levi chain runs through begetting fathers" and "I admit that no KJV verse says so" (Mary's descent). |

Defender's close round answered each pressed witness in turn — 2 Samuel 7:12: "'Father' in the register reaches by descent, not by an unbroken chain of begettings"; Acts 2:30: "The text does not make Joseph the sole channel of that descent"; Hebrews 7:10/7:5: "I grant that the loins carry through fathers in the ordinary course. The question here is whether the text gives Joseph as begetter of this child"; Matthew 1:19: "The text gives Joseph's intent and its grounds, and I do not claim a verb of knowing"; Luke 3:23: "In the two parallel verses the supposition proves wrong."

| **C3** (Joseph knew Mary within the espousal; the child of his loins) | **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** — Matthew 1:19–20, Deuteronomy 22:24, Genesis 4:1, Matthew 1:25; presented in close as a four-step chain: "So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins." |
| **C4** (two fathers in one breath = covenant pattern; the title is covenant) | **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** — 1 Chronicles 28:6, 2 Samuel 7:14, Romans 1:4, Luke 1:32, 1 John 5:1, Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34. |
| **C5** (grounds of Joseph's intent are stated in the verse) | **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** — Matthew 1:19 (*dikaios ōn*, *mē thelōn*, *eboulēthē*), Matthew 1:20 (*gar*), Luke 1:62. |
| **C6** (register by the father's house) | **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE** — "I drop the wording 'one thing' as more than the rows state." Kept to: "the register the text gives is reckoned by the father's house, and both of its lines run through Joseph." |

The challenger conceded no link. His own handling of the Jechonias bar is a citation of rows, not a construct: "The sentence is answered within the canon" (Jeremiah 18:8; Haggai 2:23; Jeremiah 22:24). On the divergence he wrote: "The text supplies the difference and does not narrate why."

No challenger link is **NO-FOOTING-EXHIBITED**.

Close rounds: the defender's close answered the challenger's R2 presses and link-round list, quoting and granting where he granted. The challenger's close pressed nothing new, and no verse named in it is a verse its earlier rounds had not already named.

---

## 3. DRIFT GUARD VIOLATIONS — CHALLENGER SEAT ONLY

**None charged.** Tested classes and the record's words:

- **Seed vs. blood / lineage verdict.** Every lineage claim the seat makes runs in the text's own word and shows the promise rows: "The oath is a seed out of David's bowels and loins, according to the flesh" (2 Samuel 7:12; Acts 2:30; Romans 1:3). No blood-word, no "ethnic outsider," no "Gentile by descent" appears anywhere in its rounds.
- **"Son of God" as covenant title.** Handled as Davidic title and resurrection declaration: "God is father by choice and title, and David is father by begetting, in one breath" (1 Chronicles 28:6; Romans 1:4). No divine-paternity reading.
- **The Holy Ghost's row.** Never read as the biological begetter, and never cut from its row; it is placed beside a father named in the text: "'Of the Holy Ghost' and 'Son of God' are covenant-origin words that stand beside a father's begetting [L2, L3]."
- **The forbidden closure.** The seat never asserts or grants "no human father," "without a man," or a Spirit-paternity for Christ. Its nearest grant stops short of it: "The passive leaves the begetting unnarrated."
- **Genealogy divergences.** Left as the text gives them: "The text supplies the difference and does not narrate why."
- **No present-day people-group is named** anywhere in the seat's rounds, and no scatter/convergence claim is made.
- **No single-stating-verse demand.** Its questions are of the form "According to Hebrews 7:14, how is it 'evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda'?" and are answered from exhibited chains.

Grants checked: nothing a guard lists as forbidden was granted, accepted at full weight, or conceded by this seat in any round.

---

## 4. HOW THE CHALLENGER ENGAGED, AND THE DEFENSE'S METHOD

- The challenger engaged chains **as chains**: six declared links, each carrying L1 text, L2 lexical anchor and L3 cross-reference; presses numbered and keyed to the link they bear on; the link round labelled each link **SUPPORTED** or **NARROWED** and answered each pressed witness by name; the close round restated the same six and pressed nothing new. It did not strip isolated terms — its objections are aimed at inferences, not at the words: "the passive names who bore him and is silent on who begat."
- It exhibited its own footing where the footing was thinnest, narrowing rather than over-claiming: "I drop the wording 'one thing' as more than the rows state."
- The defense engaged the presses and conceded on the record rather than absorbing them: "I concede three points first" (G4160; Luke 1:27's antecedent; Galatians 4:4/Genesis 3:15 as decisive); "I accept that the register runs by Joseph's house. I deny that a register entry is a proof of begetting"; and at close, his own standing: "D1, D2, D3 and D5 stand on Matthew 1:16, 1:18, 1:20 and Luke 1:34–35. D4 stands narrowed to Luke 3:23 and the acts of Matthew 1:21 and 1:24."
- **Method defect check:** the substitution sentence of the judge_fix8 type ("Noted. Not conceding here. Goes to review.") does not occur anywhere in this transcript. No round of either seat stands a label in place of an answer.

---

## 5. MOST VULNERABLE (no verdict offered; the record's words only)

**On the defender's side, the thinnest footing is the flesh-channel of the Davidic oath.** His own concessions locate it: "I admit that no KJV verse says so" (Mary's descent), and "I grant the Levi chain runs through begetting fathers." His answer is that descent in the register is not a run of begettings — "'Father' in the register reaches by descent, not by an unbroken chain of begettings" — and that "The text does not make Joseph the sole channel of that descent." Against that sit the rows the challenger presses: 2 Samuel 7:12 "which shall proceed out of thy bowels"; Acts 2:30 "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh"; Romans 1:3 "made of the seed of David according to the flesh"; Hebrews 7:10 "he was yet in the loins of his father," with the challenger's counter "It does, but the reach passes through a begetting father at every link (Matthew 1:2)," and his closing claim "The oath of Acts 2:30 and 2 Samuel 7:12, 'which shall proceed out of thy bowels,' is kept through Joseph or it is not kept." The defender's own support at this point is Luke 1:32's "the throne of his father David."

**On the challenger's side, the thinnest footing is the step from Matthew 1:19–25 to the knowing, and the last-link requirement in C1.** Matthew 1:19 states grounds and an intent and, as both seats agree, "carries no verb of knowing" — the defender's words: "The text gives Joseph's intent and its grounds, and I do not claim a verb of knowing," and "The verse does not say what he knew." The challenger's step across that gap is stated as an inference on rows: "Footed on these rows, Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins," meeting Matthew 1:18's "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost" and Matthew 1:25's bound. His C6, as he narrowed it, rests on "both of its lines run through Joseph," beside Luke 3:23's "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**Where the contest actually sits:** both seats agree Matthew 1:16 does not state a begetter — "I agree the passive does not by itself state a begetter" / "The passive leaves the begetting unnarrated" — so the contested ground is the oath rows (2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 132:11; Acts 2:30; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 7:10) set against Genesis 4:1 and Matthew 1:18–25, with the covenant-title rows (1 Chronicles 28:6; 2 Samuel 7:14; Romans 1:4) holding for the second fatherhood on both sides' filings.

(A review of the single judge's second opinion, which was HELD. The debate's verdict is the panel's.)
**ACCURATE AS A TRANSCRIPT — NOT AS A BREAK.** (1) *Accurate?* Yes on the record's surface: every concession is quoted as both seats filed it — the defender's withdrawals (*synerchomai* for G4160; Luke 1:27's antecedent; Galatians 4:4 and Genesis 3:15 as decisive; and at close Jeremiah 22:30, Ezra 2:61 and Matthew 1:25 as independent grounds), the challenger's single narrowing ("one thing"), and the jointly held bound that "till" reaches the birth and not behind the taking — and neither seat stood a note where an answer belonged. (2) *Tensions?* Two, both structural. (a) The second opinion's *break* — "it never states that Joseph begat Jesus" — is the retired single-verse ruler wearing the record's clothes: the challenger's chain was judged by whether one verse inside it says the thing in its own words, though the method is precept upon precept, here a little and there a little (Isaiah 28:10), and a chain so built has no such verse by design. The audit cures the wording by restatement, but the cure restates the form, not the weighing — a chain is measured by its exhibited links, not by whether one member states the conclusion. (b) D5 — "Christ had no biological father" — is a closure the text never issues: "of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:18, 1:20) is covenant-origin, not paternity — the defender himself granted the "of God" parallels at John 1:13 and 1 John 5:1 are said of men who had fathers — and the passive at Matthew 1:16 does not say "no man," as he conceded: "the passive does not by itself state a begetter." Silence in one verse is being run as a verdict in the other direction, against the rows the challenger exhibited and the defender did not overturn but granted: "I grant the Levi chain runs through begetting fathers," and "no KJV verse says" Mary's descent — leaving the Davidic flesh-channel (2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 132:11; Acts 2:30; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 7:14) with no exhibited channel on the defender's side. (3) *New?* Nothing new in the text; two new shapes in the record, both narrowing rather than addition — the espousal-wife footing (Deuteronomy 22:24 with Matthew 1:19–20) and the symmetric withdrawal on both sides. The break, then, is not that the challenger failed to cite; it is that the second opinion declined to weigh the chain it cited — the one move the framework exists to refuse.

**D2 stands.** The source of the conception is stated as the Holy Ghost.

**D3 stands.** The register breaks its "begat" at Joseph.

## C4 — RESTATED: Two fathers named in one breath is the covenant pattern.

- **[L1]** 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father." In one verse, the son David begat is also the son God chose.

  - "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you" (Acts 1:8) is said of the apostles;
  - "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them" (Luke 9:34) is said at the transfiguration.
- **[L4]** God is father by choice and title, and David is father by begetting, in one breath [L1, L3]. Romans 1:3-4 joins the seed according to the flesh with the title declared by the resurrection [L3]. "Of the Holy Ghost" and "Son of God" are covenant-origin words that stand beside a father's begetting [L2, L3]. They do not name a begetter in place of the named father.

## C5 — RESTATED: The ground of the intent in Matthew 1:19 is stated as "being a just man" and "not willing to make her a publick example."

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L2]** The verse gives two grounds and an intent:
  - *dikaios* (G1342, "just") and "not willing" are the two grounds;
  - *boulomai* (G1014, "was minded") is the intent.

  No verb of knowledge stands in the row.
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "But while he thought on these things ... fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel's "for" grounds the command to take her. Joseph then carries out the father's act: "thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Matthew 1:21). It is the same act Zacharias performs: "they made signs to his father, how he would have him called" (Luke 1:62).
- **[L4]** The row states what Joseph intended and why [L1, L2]. It does not state what he knew. The angel's answer sends him to take his wife and to perform the naming that belongs to the father [L3]. Nothing in this row stands against the father named in C3.

## C6 — NARROWED TO: the register the text gives is reckoned by the father's house, and both of its lines run through Joseph.

- **[L1]** Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers". Ezra 2:59: "they could not shew their father's house, and their seed" (margin "or, pedigree"). Ezra 2:62: "therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."
- **[L2]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph". *enomizeto* (G3543, "to do by law (usage) ... suppose, be wont") is the same form as Acts 16:13, "where prayer was wont to be made". The verb carries no verdict of its own, and each row's context decides it:
  - Luke 2:44, "supposing him to have been in the company";
  - Acts 14:19, "supposing he had been dead".
- **[L3]** Both lines run through Joseph:
  - Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus". This passive does not narrate the begetting.
  - Luke 3:23 runs through Joseph, and Luke 3:38 ends it: "which was [the son] of God". There the title is given to Adam, who had no human father.
- **[L4]** The text reckons pedigree by the father's house and puts out of the register those reckoned through a wife's house [L1, Ezra 2:61-62]. Both of the text's lines run through Joseph [L3]. Luke 3:23's verb takes its sense from its context [L2], and that context includes Mary's own "thy father" (Luke 2:48). So the register stands with the named father.

## The record's reading

The text answers the question from its own rows, precept upon precept (Isaiah 28:10). The answer is yes: Christ had a biological father, and the text names him. He is Joseph, "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4). Mary called him "thy father" (Luke 2:48). The town said "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph" (John 6:42). The rows join as follows:

- The oath required seed "out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12). The apostles say it was kept: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30) and "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3). Such seed comes from a father's loins (Hebrews 7:10).
- The canon's means of begetting is knowing (Genesis 4:1). Joseph and Mary were husband and wife from the espousal (Matthew 1:19, 20; Deuteronomy 22:24). The abstinence is bounded to the pregnancy (Matthew 1:25).
- "Of the Holy Ghost" and "the Son of God" are covenant words. God said of Solomon, David's own son, "I have chosen him [to be] my son" (1 Chronicles 28:6). The resurrection declares the title (Romans 1:4).

The seed is David's according to the flesh, through the named father, and the covenant Son is God's by his own oath.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** By "biological father" I mean a man who by natural generation supplies the conception of a child. The KJV says Jesus was conceived in Mary without any man. Joseph was his legal and supposed father only. The Holy Ghost is the stated source of the conception.

## 1. The source of the conception is stated

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek is *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537 + G4151 + G40): "out of the Holy Spirit". The preposition *ek* (G1537) means "out of, from as source". The text names the source of the pregnancy, and that source is not Joseph. The timing agrees: "before they came together" (Greek *synelthein*, G4905, "to come together").

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The participle *gennēthen* (G1080) means "that which is begotten or conceived". The angel tells Joseph the origin of what is in her, and he gives it as *ek pneumatos hagiou*.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the source of the pregnancy as the Holy Ghost, and Matthew 1:20 repeats the same *ek* ("of") for the conception. *Ek* denotes source, so the conception's source is the Holy Ghost, not a man. A natural father would be the *ek* of the conception, and the text assigns that role elsewhere.

## 2. Mary is called a virgin, and she says she knew no man

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name was Mary."

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means "virgin". It is used twice in this one verse of Mary.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097) means "to know", here in the sense of marital relations. Mary says *andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I know not". The verb is present tense, so she has no relations at that time.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow". *Dio* (G1352) means "therefore". The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and the angel gives that as the answer to her question "How?"

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23, quoting Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son." The Hebrew in Isaiah 7:14 is *'almah* (H5959), "virgin", which stands behind the KJV's "virgin". Matthew 1:22 introduces it: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet."

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 asks how a conception can happen with no man. Luke 1:35 answers with the Holy Ghost coming upon her, and the "therefore" ties the Son's title to that act. Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 confirm the sign is a virgin who conceives. So the conception came by the Holy Ghost, not by a man.

## 3. Joseph did not father the child

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097) with the negative *ouk*: "knew her not". The word *heōs* (G2193), "until", marks the period through the birth.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L4]** Joseph supposed something was wrong (Matthew 1:19) and was told the child's source (Matthew 1:20). He had no relations with her through the birth (Matthew 1:25). So he was not the father of the conception.

## 4. The genealogy breaks the "begat" pattern at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac." Verse 16 reads: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** *Egennēsen* (G1080, aorist active) means "begat". It is the repeated verb for the male line. In verse 16 the pattern changes to *ex hēs egennēthē* ("of whom was born"), where *hēs* ("whom") is feminine singular. The relative points to Mary, not to Joseph, and the verb is passive.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:16 gives "Joseph the husband of Mary", not "father of Jesus". The pattern "X begat Y" is dropped, and the birth is attributed to the feminine "of whom". Both the verb change and the gender mark the break, so Joseph is not the begetter.

## 5. Jesus and others speak of Joseph as father only by supposition

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543) means "was supposed, was reckoned by custom or opinion".

**[L3]** Luke 2:48 has Mary say "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Luke 2:49 gives the reply: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Jesus answers "thy father" with "my Father's".

**[L3]** Matthew 13:55: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" These are the crowd's words, not the narrator's.

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 labels the Joseph relation as "supposed". Luke 2:49 shows Jesus redirecting "father" to a different Father. So references to Joseph as father are popular or legal, and the narrator's own account (Luke 1:35, Matthew 1:20) places the conception elsewhere.

## 6. Anticipating the Davidic line

Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh." This does not make Joseph the begetter. **[L3]** Luke 1:32 says "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David", and Luke 1:27 puts Mary with Joseph in "the house of David". **[L4]** Descent from David is carried through the mother's side and the household. It is not required through a male begetter, because Matthew 1:20 already gave the conception's source and Luke 1:35 gave the cause.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. The conception of Jesus is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost", not of Joseph. [L1] Matthew 1:18 "found with child of the Holy Ghost" and Matthew 1:20 "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost"; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537), "out of the Holy Spirit", marks source; the two verses together give the chain to the conclusion.
2. Mary was a virgin and no man was involved. [L1] Luke 1:27 "a virgin... the virgin's name was Mary" and Luke 1:34 "seeing I know not a man"; [L2] *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin", and *ginōskō* (G1097), "know" in the marital sense; [L3] Luke 1:35 "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore" supplies the cause.
3. Joseph did not father the child. [L1] Matthew 1:25 "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son"; [L2] *ginōskō* (G1097) and *heōs* (G2193), "until"; [L3] Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph "minded to put her away privily" until told the source in Matthew 1:20.
4. The genealogy and the narrators treat Joseph's fatherhood as legal or supposed only. [L1] Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus"; [L2] *egennēsen* (G1080), "begat", dropped in favor of *ex hēs egennēthē*, with *hēs* feminine; [L3] Luke 3:23 "as was supposed", *enomizeto* (G3543), "was supposed".
5. Jesus had no biological father. [L1] Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 name the Holy Ghost as the source of the conception; [L3] Matthew 1:25 and Luke 1:34 exclude relations with any man; [L4] a biological father is a man who supplies the conception, and the text names no man as such, only the Holy Ghost, so Jesus had no biological father.

# Defender, Round 2 (reissued): Each press answered on its own row

I grant the setting for the pressed rows: Joseph is of the house of David (Luke 2:4) and is Mary's husband (Matthew 1:19). I hold that he is the legal and supposed father only. Each of the eight listed premises is answered below.

---

## ANSWER TO PREMISE 1 (D1): Matthew 1:20, *gar* and 1 John 5:1

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Gar* (G1063, "for") gives the ground of "fear not". What Joseph feared is in Matthew 1:19: *apolysai* (G630, "to put away"). The ground is the origin of what is in her. The object of *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate", "begotten" in the margin) in Matthew 1:20 is "that which is conceived in her", a thing in the womb.

**[L3]** Matthew 5:31: "Whosoever shall put away his wife"; Matthew 5:32: "saving for the cause of fornication." The same verb *apolyō* (G630, "put away") is used of a husband putting away a wife over fornication.

**[L4]** The press means that "of the Holy Ghost" is covenant origin tied to Joseph taking his wife. But a husband who knew himself the father would have no cause to be "minded to put her away" (Matthew 1:19). Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph had that cause, because Matthew 1:18 says she "was found with child" "before they came together". The angel's *gar* removes that cause by naming the source, and the source named is the Holy Ghost, not Joseph. Matthew 1:19, 1:18 and 5:32 stand together on this.

**1 John 5:1.** The object there is "Whosoever believeth", a person made a child of God by faith. The object in Matthew 1:20 is "that which is conceived in her". Challenger's own John 3:6 sets two origins side by side: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." Luke 1:31 puts the conceiving "in thy womb". The word for covenant sonship is not the word for what is conceived in a womb.

**Romans 1:3.** **[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." **[L3]** Romans 1:4: "declared [to be] the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness." **[L2]** The verb in Romans 1:3 is *ginomai* (G1096, "to become, to be made"), a verb of coming into being. **[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the verb "begat" for each father in the line: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob". **[L4]** Romans 1:3 says the Son "was made of the seed of David", a verb of becoming where Matthew 1:2 has the verb "begat". The same sentence gives two origins: flesh "of the seed of David", and Sonship "of God" (Romans 1:4). Romans 1:3 states descent from David, and it states it with "was made", so it is no witness that Joseph supplied the conception.

---

## ANSWER TO PREMISES 2 AND 3 (D2): Luke 1:34-35 and Isaiah 7:14

**[L1]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son." Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** "This" in Luke 1:34 refers to the conceiving of Luke 1:31. *Epei* (G1894, "seeing") gives her ground for asking: *andra ou ginōskō* (G1097, "I know not a man"). *Dio* (G1352, "therefore") in Luke 1:35 grounds the title in the clause just before it, the coming of the Holy Ghost and the overshadowing.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." The challenger's own row gives the ordinary means: knowing, then conceiving. Mary's "seeing I know not a man" asks how conception can come without that means. Luke 1:35 answers with the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest.

**[L4]** The challenger's verbs prove only that the words have range. On Luke 9:34 and Acts 1:8, the challenger said in Round 1 that "context decides what the verb carries." Here the context is a question about conceiving ("thou shalt conceive," Luke 1:31) and an answer from the Holy Ghost, and the result is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee." In Acts 1:8 the result is "ye shall be witnesses." The same verb *eperchomai* (G1904, "come upon") ends differently because the context differs. Luke 1:35 says "come upon thee" and then "born of thee", so the context gives a conception.

**Present tense.** The challenger says *ginōskō* is her state at the espousal. That is granted. The question concerns the coming conception ("shalt conceive," Luke 1:31), and the angel answers it with the Holy Ghost, not with a husband.

**Psalm 2:7 and 1 Chronicles 28:6.** **[L1]** Acts 13:33: "in that he hath raised up Jesus again... Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee." **[L4]** That row ties "begotten" to the raising up. Luke 1:35 ties the title to the coming of the Holy Ghost before birth ("shall be born of thee"). In 1 Chronicles 28:6, David is named as "thy son" beside "I will be his father." The sources named for Jesus are "thee" and the Holy Ghost (Luke 1:35).

**Isaiah 7:14.** **[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive." Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child."

**[L2]** *'Almah* (H5959): the sheet gives "damsel, maid, virgin", so "virgin" is within its range. *Parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") in Matthew 1:23 is the word that stands behind the KJV's "virgin" there.

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth". This is *'almah* said of Rebekah, whom Genesis 24:16 calls "a virgin, neither had any man known her." One woman receives both words. Exodus 2:8 "the maid" does not narrow the sense of Isaiah 7:14 any more than "the virgin" in Genesis 24:43 widens it. Each row's context decides.

**Isaiah 8:3.** **[L1]** Isaiah 8:3: "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz." Isaiah 7:14: "shall call his name Immanuel." **[L2]** Isaiah 8:3 has *nebiy'ah* (H5031, "prophetess"), a different word from *'almah* (H5959). **[L4]** The child of Isaiah 8:3 is given a different name from the child of Isaiah 7:14, so the rows name two children, and the woman of Isaiah 8:3 carries a different Hebrew word from the woman of Isaiah 7:14. Matthew 1:22-23 applies "a virgin shall be with child" to Mary, whom Luke 1:27 calls "a virgin" (*parthenos*) and who says in Luke 1:34, "I know not a man."

---

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** *Synelthein* (G4905, "come together") is dated before the finding. *Heōs* (G2193, "till") bounds the abstinence at the birth.

**[L4]** The challenger's order is: finding (1:18), taking (1:24), not knowing until the birth (1:25). Matthew 1:18 dates the finding "before they came together", and Matthew 1:25 dates Joseph's not knowing her up to the birth. The challenger's C5 needs Joseph to have known Mary before the finding, within the espousal. That act is supplied by the challenger's own L4. The rows give a pregnancy found before they came together (1:18), a source named by the angel (1:20), and no knowing from the taking to the birth (1:25). That leaves no point in the rows where Joseph begot.

**Matthew 1:19.** The challenger gives Joseph's two grounds as "just" and "not willing to make her a publick example", and both fit my reading. The "public example" would be made of her, and the thing that would make her one is the pregnancy found "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18). Mark 7:8 speaks of "the washing of pots and cups" and "the tradition of men", and it is a row about washing, not betrothal. Joseph's own verb is *apolysai* (G630), the husband's word for putting away a wife (Matthew 5:31), and "saving for the cause of fornication" (Matthew 5:32) shows what putting away answers. So Joseph's mind in Matthew 1:19 is the mind of a man who is not the father.

---

## ANSWER TO PREMISE 6 (D4): Matthew 1:16, Luke 3:23, Luke 2:48

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."

**[L2]** *Egennēsen* (G1080, "begat", active) governs every link of the line, as in Matthew 1:2. The last clause is *ex hēs egennēthē* (feminine relative, passive). The challenger grants that it "names the mother who bore him."

**[L4]** Each earlier link is "X begat Y", with a male subject for the active verb. The one link where the subject is Joseph breaks to "the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus". The clause that gives the birth has the feminine "of whom" and the passive "was born", and it names the mother as the one of whom he was born.

**Luke 3:23.** **[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543, "was supposed"). **[L3]** The challenger cites Luke 2:44: "supposing him to have been in the company." Luke 2:45: "And when they found him not." **[L4]** In the challenger's own witness, the same verb names a supposition that proved wrong. KJV Luke 3:23 gives "supposed" as the English. Luke inserts "(as was supposed)" to qualify "the son of Joseph". If Joseph were the begetter, nothing would need qualifying.

**Luke 2:48 and the narrator.** **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" **[L3]** Luke 2:43: "Joseph and his mother knew not of it." Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled." **[L4]** Mary calls Joseph "thy father" in the household sense, and Jesus answers with "my Father's business." Luke's narrator, when naming Joseph apart, writes "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33, 2:43), and uses "the parents" (Luke 2:27) and "his parents" (Luke 2:41) of the household. That is the household's name for them, and Luke 3:23 qualifies it with "as was supposed."

**The crowd and the disciple.** **[L1]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" **[L4]** The speakers' "we know" is followed by their own puzzlement at his claim. John 1:45 is Philip's report. The narrator's account is Luke 1:35.

---

## ANSWER TO PREMISES 7 AND 8 (D5): the seed rows and Hebrews 7:14

**[L1]** Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ." Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." Hebrews 7:5: "they come out of the loins of Abraham."

**[L4]** Hebrews 7:5 says the Levites "come out of the loins of Abraham", and Hebrews 7:10 says Levi "was yet in the loins of his father" when Abraham met Melchisedec. Both rows use "loins" for a forefather's body across the generations between. So "the fruit of his loins" (Acts 2:30), "out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12) and "of the seed of David" (Romans 1:3) give the sense "a descendant of David", and the child "born of thee" (Luke 1:35) is that descendant by his mother.

Matthew 1:18 says "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Which quoted row places Joseph's knowing of Mary before that finding? Your C5 needs that act, and the order you accepted (1:18, 1:24, 1:25) has no place for it.

## 1. Uncontested textual points

These are limited to points not themselves contested in either side’s charge list; they do not decide the disputed chains.

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:21 assigns Joseph the naming: “thou shalt call his name JESUS.”
- **[L1]** Deuteronomy 25:6 states that the firstborn “shall succeed in the name of his brother.” The sides disputed what this contributes to their arguments.
- **[L3]** Both sides used Genesis 4:1 as an example of a husband knowing his wife followed by conception; they disputed its application to Joseph and Mary.

## 2. Link-round results and contested chains

The classifications below record **whether footing was exhibited**, not whether an inference follows from it. Citation of two layers is not, by itself, proof of a link.

### Defender’s links

| **D3: Joseph’s abstinence** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger placed Matthew 1:25’s abstinence after the taking in verse 24 and argued for knowing during the espousal. It granted: “I grant ‘born of thee’ names her as the mother.” It argued that the result clause’s main verb is “shall be called.” The defender appealed to the conception question in Luke 1:31, 34 and to Matthew 1:20. |
| **C5: David’s house on Joseph** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger cited Luke 1:27; 2:4, 48; and Matthew 1:20. It granted that the angel calls David the child’s father and that God is the actor in 2 Samuel 7:12. The defender maintained its narrowed chain through Mary. |

Neither link round records a whole link as **CONCEDED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE** or **NO-FOOTING-EXHIBITED**. The grants quoted above concern particular premises or textual observations, not withdrawals of whole links.

### Close rounds

The defender’s close addressed the previously pressed witnesses on the timing, Luke’s annunciation, Joseph’s intended action, the genealogy, Mary’s “thy father,” David’s seed and Hebrews’ likeness language. Its reference to **Hebrews 4:15** is excluded under the supplied new-verse check. Sentences in that close that press or grade challenger links are also excluded under the supplied close-round rule.

The challenger’s close restated its chain, grants and chronology objection. The defender had no subsequent round; that procedural silence is not a concession. The sentence identified by the supplied challenger close-round check is disregarded as a press.

On chronology, the defender had granted that the taking follows the finding and that Matthew 1:25 then says Joseph “knew her not.” Its close also said: “The not-knowing spans the conceiving.” The challenger identified that as a contradiction. The distinction is that the earlier grant describes the sequence narrated; it does not expressly say abstinence **began only** at the taking. Whether the later statement is established by the cited sequence remains contested.

## 3. Challenger’s conduct against the supplied constraints

No explicit violation is identified in the challenger’s quoted claims or grants. In particular, its grants that Matthew’s “begat” line reaches Joseph and that Mary is the mother did not withdraw its claim about Joseph. The defender, as the plain seat, is not assessed against those constraints.

## 4. Engagement and remaining pressure points

Both sides exhibited chains and responded to opposing cross-references; neither link round used the placeholder described in the request. Their recurring dispute was not simply over isolated words, but over **what the links permit**:

- whether the timing in Matthew 1:18, 24–25 places or excludes a knowing during the espousal;
- whether “of the Holy Ghost” in Matthew 1:18, 20 bears the source inference each side assigns it;
- whether Davidic seed and Joseph’s named house establish the particular route each side proposes;
- whether Hebrews 2’s likeness extends to the means of conception.

Those are the load-bearing contested points in the record. No outcome is assigned here.

# DEFENDER'S OPENING

I open and defend the standard reading of the record: Christ had no biological father. The record states the source of the child in Mary's womb, states the time of that conception, states the mother's own condition, and states Joseph's conduct through the birth. I present that case now, link by link, with its layers.

## THE QUESTION IN THE RECORD'S OWN WORDS

The record's own idiom for a biological father is a man's knowing and begetting:

[L1] Genesis 4:1 — "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD." [L2] יָדַע, yada (H3045, knew — the verb of a man knowing his wife); וַתַּהַר, vattahar, from הָרָה, harah (H2030, conceived); וַתֵּלֶד, vatteled, from יָלַד, yalad (H3205, bare).

[L1] Matthew 1:2 — "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;" [L2] ἐγέννησεν, egennēsen, from γεννάω, gennaō (G1080, beget — the father's part).

[L4] CHAIN: On Genesis 4:1 [L1] with yada, harah, yalad [L2], and Matthew 1:2 [L1] with gennaō [L2], the frame of this question in the record's own words: a biological father is the man who knows the woman and begets the child. My case is that for this child the record states the source otherwise.

## LINK 1 — The begetting-list changes its own stated formula at Jesus

[L1] Matthew 1:16 — "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] ἐξ ἧς, ex hēs — "of whom": ἐκ, ek (G1537, out of, from — the preposition of source) joined to the feminine relative pronoun ἧς, hēs (of her), whose stated antecedent is Mary, the last-named person; ἐγεννήθη, egennēthē, from gennaō (G1080, was begotten, born).

[L3] Matthew 1:15 — "And Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob;" — the entry immediately before, in the list's standing formula "X begat Y" (gennaō, beget).

[L4] CHAIN: From Matthew 1:2 to Matthew 1:15 the list states its formula as "X begat Y," father to son, with gennaō [L2] standing in Matthew 1:2 [L1] and Matthew 1:15 [L3]. At Jesus the stated formula changes: Joseph is begotten by Jacob, but Jesus is "born of" — ex hēs, of her — Mary. The record's own wording stops the begetting-chain at Joseph and carries this child's birth through the mother, marked with the source-preposition ek and the feminine "of her."

## LINK 2 — The stated source: "of the Holy Ghost," before union

[L1] Matthew 1:18 — "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

## 1. Uncontested textual floor

These points were not themselves charged in either side’s premise list:

- **[L1]** Genesis 4:1 states that Adam knew Eve, and she conceived and bore Cain.
- **[L1]** Joseph is called Mary’s husband and addressed as a son of David (Matthew 1:19–20).
- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:14 says the Lord sprang out of Juda. Both sides addressed how that statement relates to the fathers’ houses in Numbers 1:2, 18.

Other major textual claims were drawn into at least one charge. Their disputed applications are recorded below rather than placed on the uncontested floor.

## 2. Link rounds and close rounds

**Status key:** CITED-WITH-FOOTING records that a side exhibited at least two prior layers and a proposed connection. It is a procedural description, not a finding that the connection succeeds. CONCEDED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE requires an express concession of the link; NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE requires a limb to be dropped while the link is kept.

### Defender’s six charged links

| Link | Status | Both sides’ answers |
|---|---|---|
| **D1 — Matthew 1:16’s formula** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The defender cited the change from active begetting to the feminine relative and passive birth. The challenger cited Genesis 4:25 and Galatians 4:4: naming the mother does not itself exclude a father. The defender kept the formula-change claim and relied on the other conception passages for its wider inference. |
| **D2 — “of the Holy Ghost”** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The defender joined Matthew 1:18, 20 to the timing and source language, with 1 Corinthians 7:5. The challenger joined Matthew 1:20 to John 1:13 and the named husband. The defender distinguished John’s believers from Matthew’s conception narrative. |
| **D3 — Luke’s question and answer** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The defender read Luke 1:31, 34–35 as a chain about the promised conception. The challenger cited Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34 for the range of “come upon” and “overshadow,” and the Davidic title passages for the calling. The defender answered that those other occurrences have different subjects. |
| **D4 — the period of not-knowing** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The defender joined Matthew 1:18, 24–25 and 1 Corinthians 7:5. The challenger located the not-knowing after the taking and argued for an earlier knowing. The defender replied that the finding and the not-knowing delimit the relevant sequence. |
| **D5 — the Hebrew usage point** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The defender cited Genesis 24:16, 43 for one woman described both by the Hebrew word and as not known by a man. The challenger cited Isaiah 7:14, 16 and 8:3 for the immediate setting and the word’s range. The defender retained Matthew 1:22–23 alongside that setting. |
| **D6 — the overall fatherhood inference** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The defender assembled D1–D5 and Luke 3:23. The challenger pressed Romans 1:3, 2 Samuel 7:12, Luke 2:48 and Hebrews 7:14. The defender answered with Joseph’s house, the genealogy’s wording, and a distinction between the house account and conception account. |

### Challenger’s six charged links

| Link | Status | Both sides’ answers |
|---|---|---|
| **C1 — Spirit and flesh; mixed kinds** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger joined Matthew 1:20, John 3:6, 1 John 5:1 and Leviticus 19:19. The defender distinguished the new-birth setting and the statute’s named subjects, citing Genesis 2:7 and Hebrews 10:5 as well. The challenger retained its cross-reference. |
| **C2 — “come upon” and “overshadow”** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger cited Luke 1:35, Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34. The defender pressed Luke 1:31, 34–35’s immediate question-and-answer setting. The challenger retained the comparison with the other uses. |
| **C3 — the “therefore” and Son-title** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger joined Luke 1:32–35 to 2 Samuel 7:14 and 1 Chronicles 28:6. The defender pressed the order within Luke 1:35 while granting the title passages. The challenger retained its reading of the connection. |
| **C4 — knowing within the espousal** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger joined Genesis 4:1 and Matthew 1:19–20, 25, with Luke 2:7. The defender pressed Matthew 1:18, 24–25 and 1 Corinthians 7:5. The challenger distinguished the coming together from the knowing and retained its proposed sequence. |
| **C5 — the father-naming chain** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger joined Luke 2:48, Luke 1:32 and John 6:42. The defender cited Luke 2:49 and 3:23 and the range of “father.” The challenger retained Mary’s naming alongside the Davidic line. |
| **C6 — seed and the fathers’ house** | CITED-WITH-FOOTING | The challenger joined Hebrews 7:14 and Numbers 1:2, 18 to 2 Samuel 7:12, Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30. The defender answered with Joseph’s house and Matthew 1:16 and Luke 3:23. The challenger retained its flesh-seed chain. |

**Concessions and narrowings:** Neither side expressly conceded one of its six charged links or expressly withdrew a limb while retaining a link. Both link rounds labelled all six of their own links supported; the tables above report the exhibited footing rather than adopt those labels as substantive findings.

The defender did make textual grants. Examples include its acceptance of Mary’s words in **Luke 2:48**, “thy father and I,” and of **Romans 1:3**, “the seed of David according to the flesh.” Those grants did not concede the challenger’s complete inference.

In the defender’s close, it responded to the earlier presses across the genealogy, conception, knowing, Isaiah, father-naming and seed passages. The challenger’s final close had no further press; its position in the sequence creates no concession by either side.

## 3. Challenger’s guard review

No express violation is established by the challenger’s **own** grants or assertions in this transcript.

The challenger’s final grant list reproduces the defender’s reading of **Matthew 1:25**, “knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son,” but labels the associated grants as supporting **“none”** and identifies them as the defender’s reading. Reproducing the quotation in that form is not, by itself, an acceptance of the defender’s inference.

The challenger’s mixed-kinds application of **Leviticus 19:19** was explicitly pressed by the defender and retained by the challenger as an [L4] chain. That disagreement is recorded above; its presence alone does not establish an express concession or an independently demonstrated guard violation.

## 4. Engagement and method

The challenger engaged the defense as a chain: it pressed the seed, naming, timing, Spirit and title links separately, then retained its own six chains through the link round. The defender likewise responded link by link and revisited the cited witnesses in its close.

Both sides exhibited citations and proposed connections. Repeated declarations that a witness “fits” or a link remains kept do not themselves settle the disputed connection. The record contains no placeholder of the kind identified in the instruction.

## 5. Most vulnerable connections

- **Defender’s timeline:** the movement from **Matthew 1:18**, “before they came together,” and **Matthew 1:25**, “knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son,” to the complete proposed sequence.
- **Challenger’s timeline:** the movement from **Genesis 4:1**, “Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived,” and **Matthew 1:25** to knowing within the espousal before the finding.
- **Both seed arguments:** the connection between **Romans 1:3**, “the seed of David according to the flesh,” and the particular account of Joseph’s relation to Jesus in **Matthew 1:16** and **Luke 3:23**.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Thesis.** The KJV presents Mary as the only human parent of Christ. His conception was "of the Holy Ghost." Joseph was his legal and supposed father, not his begetter. This is the standard reading, and I defend it as a chain, not as isolated verses.

## 1. The genealogy breaks its own pattern

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-15 runs on one verb, "begat," from Abraham to Jacob. Then Matthew 1:16 reads: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb in the pattern is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "he begat"), active, with a man as subject. In Matthew 1:16 the verb changes to ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born"), passive. The relative pronoun is ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), feminine singular. It can refer only to Mary, not to Joseph, who is called ἄνδρα (andra, "husband, man") of Mary.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2-15 supplies the pattern. Matthew 1:16 departs from it exactly where Jesus is reached. Joseph is never said to have begotten him.

## 2. The source of the conception is stated

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The phrase is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Holy Spirit"). ἐκ (ek, "out of") names source or origin. The participle is γεννηθέν (gennēthen, "that which is begotten or conceived"), the same root as the genealogy's verb. The text assigns the begetting to the Holy Ghost, not to Joseph.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The verbs are ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "shall come upon") and ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "shall overshadow"). The phrase "therefore also" ties the title to this mode of conception. Matthew and Luke state the same fact independently.

## 3. Mary's virginity excludes a human father

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Matthew 1:18 places the conception "before they came together." Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** The verb in Luke 1:34 is γινώσκω (ginōskō, "to know"), used of marital relations. Matthew 1:25 has ἐγίνωσκεν ... ἕως οὗ (eginōsken ... heōs hou, "was knowing ... until which"), so the birth took place while she was a virgin. For Isaiah 7:14, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive," the Hebrew is עַלְמָה (ʿalmāh, "young woman of marriageable age, maiden"). Matthew 1:23 renders it παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin").

**[L3]** The KJV renders the same Hebrew word "virgin" in Genesis 24:43, of Rebekah, whom Genesis 24:16 describes as "a virgin, neither had any man known her." Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in this birth. Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed," the woman's seed, with no male named.

## 4. Joseph's fatherhood is only supposed

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." In Matthew 1:19 Joseph, on learning of the pregnancy, "was minded to put her away privily." He knew the child was not his.

**[L2]** ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed, reckoned") marks opinion or legal reckoning, not fact. Without the parenthesis the verse would have said ὤν (ōn, "being") alone.

**[L3]** The objections come from people who spoke from appearance. John 6:42 says, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Luke 2:48, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing," is Mary's household usage. Christ answers in Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" That corrects the question of whose son he is. Galatians 4:4 says "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." The Greek γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "coming to be out of a woman") names the woman alone. Hebrews 10:5 says "a body hast thou prepared me," from κατηρτίσω (katartisō, "fitted, prepared").

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern of Matthew 1:2-15: the active ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") gives way to the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") with feminine ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"). Joseph is therefore not credited with begetting Jesus. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16; [L2] the verb and pronoun forms; [L3] the pattern of Matthew 1:2-15.
2. The text names the Holy Ghost as the source of the conception: ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Holy Spirit") in Matthew 1:18,20, confirmed by "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" in Luke 1:35. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18,20; [L2] ἐκ and γεννηθέν; [L3] Luke 1:35.
3. Mary was a virgin at conception, so no human male was involved: Luke 1:34 "I know not a man" and Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till she had brought forth." Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34, Matthew 1:25; [L2] ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing") and παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Genesis 24:16,43 on עַלְמָה (ʿalmāh, "young woman, maiden").
4. Joseph's fatherhood is legal and reputed only: Luke 3:23 "as was supposed," with ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed"). Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23, Matthew 1:19; [L2] ἐνομίζετο; [L3] Luke 2:48-49, John 6:42, Galatians 4:4.
5. Christ had no human biological father. His human parentage is Mary alone, and his conception was of the Holy Ghost. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16,18,20, Luke 1:34-35; [L2] ἐξ ἧς, ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "coming to be out of a woman"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23, Galatians 4:4, Hebrews 10:5.
