rows.synthesis:
### 1. What held at L1-L2-L3?

A point is listed here only if no charge in either side's lists contests it; every contested point appears under section 2.

- **[L1]** In Matthew 1:20, Joseph is addressed as "Joseph, thou son of David," and in Luke 2:4, he is identified as being "of the house and lineage of David."
- **[L1]** Mary was "espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary" (Luke 1:27).
- **[L1]** In Deuteronomy 20:7, the law marks a distinction between betrothal and taking: "what man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her?"
- **[L1]** In Deuteronomy 22:23–24, a betrothed woman is described: "If a damsel that is a virgin be betrothed unto an husband... because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife."
- **[L1]** In Numbers 1:18, the pedigrees of Israel are declared "after their families, by the house of their fathers."
- **[L1]** In Ezra 2:61–62, priests who "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name" sought their register, "but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."
- **[L1]** In 1 Chronicles 28:6, the LORD says of Solomon: "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father."
- **[L1]** In 2 Samuel 7:14, the promise states: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."
- **[L1]** Psalm 2:7 ("Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee") is cited in the New Testament at Acts 13:33 in connection with the resurrection ("in that he hath raised up Jesus again"), at Hebrews 5:5 in connection with the high priesthood ("to be made an high priest"), and at Hebrews 1:5 alongside 2 Samuel 7:14 ("I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son").
- **[L1]** Romans 1:4 reads: "declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead."
- **[L1]** John 4:24 states: "God is a Spirit."
- **[L1]** Luke 24:39 states: "a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have."
- **[L1]** 1 John 5:1 states: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God: and every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him."
- **[L1]** John 1:12–13 states: "as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God... Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- **[L1]** In Luke 1:62–63, the naming of John is referred to his father: "they made signs to his father, how he would have him called... And he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John."
- **[L1]** In Acts 16:13, the Greek verb *nomizō* appears as "where prayer was wont to be made."

---

### 2. Concessions, Links, and Contested Points

#### Defender Links (D1–D6)

- **LINK D1 (Matthew 1:18, 20: conception source is the Holy Ghost before coming together):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Challenger Press:* Contested under C2 and P2.2. Challenger argues that "before they came together" designates the formal taking of Matthew 1:24 (cf. Deuteronomy 20:7), while Mary and Joseph were already husband and wife in law during espousal (Matthew 1:19; Deuteronomy 22:24), during which Joseph knew Mary per Genesis 4:1. Challenger further pressed that "of the Holy Ghost" (*ek*) marks covenant birth/origin as used in 1 John 5:1 and John 1:13 for believers who have human fathers.
  - *Defender Answer:* In [CR3] and [CR4], Defender answered that Matthew 1:18 places the finding with child "before they came together," so that placing a knowing prior to that finding contradicts the order of Matthew 1:18; that Joseph being minded to put Mary away privily (Matthew 1:19) shows he was not the source of the conception; and that *gennaō* in Matthew 1:20 ("that which is conceived [margin: begotten] in her is of the Holy Ghost") assigns begetting to the Holy Ghost, whereas John 1:13 explicitly contrasts "of God" with "of the will of man."
- **LINK D2 (Matthew 1:16: genealogy changes formula at Joseph to Mary):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Challenger Press:* Contested under C1 and P1.2. Challenger argues that *ex hēs egennēthē* names the mother's bearing within a clause that names her husband Joseph, parallel to "born of women" (Matthew 11:11; Galatians 4:4; Job 14:1) where fathers exist, and that Matthew 1:17 counts generations to Christ through Joseph.
  - *Defender Answer:* In [CR3] and [CR4], Defender answered that verses 2–15 maintain the active formula "X begat Y" with a named male subject, but verse 16 shifts to the feminine singular pronoun *hēs* and passive *egennēthē*, breaking the begetting formula specifically at Joseph; and that generational counts by register can reckon through marriage (Ezra 2:61) without begetting.
- **LINK D3 (Luke 1:34–35: Holy Ghost and power of the Highest cause conception):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Challenger Press:* Contested under C3 and P3.1. Challenger argues that "I know not a man" (Luke 1:34) states Mary's present condition at the visit; that "come upon" (*eperchomai*) and "overshadow" (*episkiazō*) signify empowerment and presence as in Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34, and Acts 5:15, rather than physical begetting; and that "therefore also" (*dio kai*) connects back to the title "Son of the Highest" and Davidic throne announced in Luke 1:32 before Mary's question.
  - *Defender Answer:* In [CR3] and [CR4], Defender answered that Mary's question "How shall this be" receives the explicit answer "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee"; that the effect stated in Luke 1:35 is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee"; and that *dio kai* directly joins that divine overshadowing to the title "Son of God."
- **LINK D4 (Matthew 1:24–25: Joseph knew her not till birth; naming is legal):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Challenger Press:* Contested under C2 and P2.3. Challenger argues that "knew her not till she had brought forth" bounds abstinence strictly to the pregnancy following the taking in Matthew 1:24, leaving open knowing within the prior espousal; and that naming is the act of a begetting father (Luke 1:62–63).
  - *Defender Answer:* In [CR3] and [CR4], Defender answered that Matthew 1:25 follows the taking (v. 24) and the finding before coming together (v. 18), establishing non-union; that the child is called "her firstborn son"; and that naming was also commanded directly to Mary (Luke 1:31; Isaiah 7:14), showing naming does not convey begetting.
- **LINK D5 (Luke 3:23: fatherhood of Joseph marked as supposed):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Challenger Press:* Contested under C1 and Link 5. Challenger argues that *enomizeto* refers to legal usage or custom as in Acts 16:13; that Mary calls Joseph "thy father" (Luke 2:48); and that the narrator repeatedly calls them "parents" (*goneus*, Luke 2:27, 41) and "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33).
  - *Defender Answer:* In [CR3] and [CR4], Defender answered that Luke 3:23 provides the inspired narrator's own qualifying aside ("as was supposed") regarding the popular attribution; that in Luke 2:48–49 Jesus counters Mary's "thy father" with "my Father's business"; and that the narrator's terms in Luke 2 reflect legal and household custom.
- **LINK D6 (Hebrews 10:5; Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:22–23; divine fatherhood without bodily seed):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Challenger Press:* Contested under C1, C4, C5, C6. Challenger pressed with Romans 1:3 ("seed of David according to the flesh"), Acts 2:30 ("fruit of his loins"), 2 Samuel 7:12 ("proceed out of thy bowels"), Hebrews 2:14 ("took part of the same"), and Jeremiah 22:30 / Haggai 2:23 (the royal line and signet).
  - *Defender Answer:* In [CR3] and [CR4], Defender answered that Romans 1:3 uses *ginomai* ("was made") and Galatians 4:4 says "made of a woman," tracing flesh to Mary; that Hebrews 10:5 states "a body hast thou prepared me"; that Hebrews 7:5, 10 demonstrate that "loins" expresses lineal descent across generations rather than immediate paternal begetting; and that Jeremiah 22:30 excludes the physical seed of Jechonias from David's throne, which would bar Christ if he were the biological seed of Joseph (Matthew 1:12, 16).

---

#### Challenger Links (C1–C6)

- **LINK C1 ("made of a woman" names Mary, and "seed of David" names what came from the father's side):** CITED-WITH-FOOTING.
  - *Defender Press:* In [CR3] P1, Defender pressed that Romans 1:3 uses *ginomai* ("was made") rather than *gennaō*, showing the line entered rather than an immediate begetting act; that Matthew 1:16 diverts the begetting formula to Mary; and that Matthew 1:20 assigns the conception to the Holy Ghost.
  - *Challenger Answer:* In [CR3], Challenger answered that *ginomai* joined with *ek spermatos* ("of the seed") denotes physical derivation, with *sperma* denoting seed including male seed; that Hebrews 7:10 places seed in the father's loins; and that Matthew 1:20's "of the Holy Ghost" reflects covenant birth as in 1 John 5:1.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: the child had no biological father

**Definition.** "Biological father" means a man whose seed contributed to the child's conception. The question is whether the KJV says Christ had one. It says he did not.

## I. The conception is traced to the Holy Ghost, not to a man

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** "Before they came together" is *prin ē synelthein autous*: before they came together (as husband and wife). The text excludes union with Joseph before the conception.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** "Conceived" is *gennēthen*, from *gennaō* (to beget, generate). It is the same verb the genealogy uses of each father. The source here is *ek pneumatos hagiou*: out of the Holy Ghost. The verb that elsewhere names a human father's act names a source that is not a man.
- **[L1]** Luke 1:34-35: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The answer: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L2]** *Ginōskō* (to know) in "I know not a man" is the Hebrew-idiom word for marital intimacy. Mary's question asks how the conception could occur without it. The answer gives a means with no man in it. *Episkiazō* (to overshadow, cast a shadow over) is a word of divine presence, not of human union. "Born of thee" is *ek sou*: out of thee, from her alone.
- **[L3]** Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her." This is the same idiom of "knowing" that Luke 1:34 uses.

## II. Matthew 1:16 breaks the genealogy's pattern at the exact point

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L2]** Every earlier line reads *egennēsen* (begat), active, father to son. For Jesus the verb becomes passive, *egennēthē* (was born), with the relative pronoun *hēs* (of whom), feminine singular. It points to Mary alone and cannot include Joseph. Joseph is called only "the husband of Mary," never the one who begat.
- **[L3]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** The word is *enomizeto* (was supposed, reckoned by custom), which marks the common belief as not the fact.

## III. Prophecy requires a virgin, and the text applies it to Mary

- **[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." Matthew 1:23 quotes it: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
- **[L2]** Hebrew *ʿalmāh* is a young woman of marriageable age, not yet married. **[L3]** Genesis 24:43 uses it of Rebekah ("when the virgin cometh forth to draw water"), whom Genesis 24:16 had already called a virgin who had known no man. Greek *parthenos* (virgin) in Matthew 1:23 fixes the sense, and Luke 1:27 calls Mary "the virgin."
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." **[L2]** *Ginōskō* (to know) is the same verb as in Luke 1:34. Joseph did not know her until after the birth.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19: Joseph, "being a just man," was "minded to put her away privily." He knew the child was not his, and the angel did not tell him otherwise. The angel confirmed it (Matthew 1:20).

## IV. The rest of Scripture speaks as if no man is the father

- **[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." **[L2]** *Genomenon ek gynaikos* means coming to be out of a woman, with no man named.
- **[L3]** Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed." **[L2]** The Hebrew is *zeraʿ* (seed), here attributed to the woman, which is unusual.
- **[L1]** Luke 2:48-49. Mary says, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." The child answers, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" **[L4]** This is a correction of the term "father." It rests on [L1] Luke 2:49 and on the contrast with Luke 3:23, where "as was supposed" marks the common belief. Together they show the child redirecting "father" away from Joseph.
- **[L3]** John 6:42 ("whose father and mother we know") and Matthew 13:55 ("the carpenter's son") are the crowd's assumptions, the same ones Luke 3:23 marks as "supposed."

## V. A biological father in Joseph's line would bar the throne

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:12 puts Jechonias in Joseph's line. **[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 says "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
- **[L3]** Luke 1:32 promises the child "the throne of his father David." **[L4]** If Joseph's seed were the child's, Jeremiah 22:30 would bar him from the throne that Luke 1:32 promises. This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:12 and Jeremiah 22:30, and on [L3] the Luke 1:32 promise. A conception with no seed of Joseph fits both texts.

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:18, 1:20), *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of the Holy Ghost). Luke 1:34-35 gives a means with no man in it, with Mary's "I know not a man" answered by "overshadow," *episkiazō* (to overshadow). **[L1][L2]**
2. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern at Jesus (*egennēsen* becomes *egennēthē*, was born), and the feminine *hēs* (of whom) makes Mary alone the source. Luke 3:23, *enomizeto* (was supposed), marks Joseph's fatherhood as presumed only. **[L1][L2][L3]**
3. Isaiah 7:14 (*ʿalmāh*, young unmarried woman, confirmed by Genesis 24:16, 24:43) is applied in Matthew 1:23 as *parthenos* (virgin). Matthew 1:25 ("knew her not till she had brought forth") shows Joseph did not know her before the birth. **[L1][L2][L3]**
4. Galatians 4:4 ("made of a woman," *ek gynaikos*, out of a woman) and Luke 2:49 ("my Father's business") redirect fatherhood away from Joseph. John 6:42 and Matthew 13:55 give only the crowd's assumption. **[L1][L2][L3]**
5. Jechonias stands in Joseph's line (Matthew 1:12), and Jeremiah 22:30 bars his seed from David's throne, which Luke 1:32 promises to the child. A conception with no seed of Joseph resolves both. **[L1][L3][L4]**
6. Therefore Christ had no biological father. His conception was "of the Holy Ghost" in the virgin Mary, and Joseph was the husband of Mary, not the one who begat. **[L1][L2][L3][L4]**

# Challenger's opening — the seed rows decide this, and they name a man

The definition is accepted: a biological father is a man whose seed contributed to the conception. On that definition the question is narrow — does the KJV say a man's seed produced the child? It says the opposite of the defence at five anatomical places, and it names the man. I aim at D6 (the keystone), then D5, D1, D2, D4, D3.

---

## I. Against D6 — the promise requires seed out of a man's body, and the canon says so in the flesh

The defence's keystone is an inference from silence ("no man named"). Here is what the text positively states.

- **[L1]** 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, **which shall proceed out of thy bowels**, and I will establish his kingdom."
- **[L1]** Psalm 132:11: "**Of the fruit of thy body** will I set upon thy throne."
- **[L1]** Romans 1:3: "Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was **made of the seed of David according to the flesh**."
- **[L1]** Acts 2:30: "that **of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh**, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
- **[L1]** 2 Timothy 2:8: "Remember that Jesus Christ **of the seed of David** was raised from the dead according to my gospel."
- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For **it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda**."

Bowels, fruit of the body, loins, flesh, sprung out of Judah, evident. That is not covenant metaphor; it is anatomical language about descent. A conception with no man's seed leaves those five rows with no referent.

**How it is "evident."** The reckoning rule:
- **[L1]** Numbers 1:2: "after their families, **by the house of their fathers**, with the number of their names, every male by their polls."

# SYNTHESIS — chain-scoped debate: "Did Christ have a biological father?"

Both sides accepted one definition at the top, and the whole debate then turned on a single chronological question that both sides answered from the same three rows in opposite order. That is the shape to keep in view while reading the statuses below.

---

## 1. What held at L1–L2–L3 (no charge from either premise list contests it)

- **[L1] The definition.** "A man whose seed contributed to the conception" (DEFENDER R1); "The definition is accepted" (CHALLENGER R1). Both sides then argued the same narrow question.
- **[L1][L2] Matthew 1:16's grammar.** *egennēsen* (active) through vv. 2–15, *egennēthē* (passive) at v. 16, *hēs* feminine singular. Both sides agree the relative names Mary as the one "of whom" Jesus was born, and that the verse does not say "Joseph begat Jesus." The challenger charged only the exclusion inference; the grammar stands.
- **[L1] Joseph's standing and descent.** "Joseph her husband" (Matt 1:19); "Mary thy wife" (1:20); "took unto him his wife" (1:24); "espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David" (Luke 1:27); "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4). Neither side disputes the words; the dispute is what the words make him.
- **[L2] The lexical range of *eperchomai* / *episkiazō*.** DEFENDER R4: "I grant that for those rows." No row of either verb narrates a conception (Acts 1:8; Matt 17:5; Luke 9:34; Acts 5:15; 1 Sam 16:13). The application to Luke 1:35 is contested; the range is not.
- **[L2] *enomizeto* can be neutral.** DEFENDER R3: "I concede that." Both sides now cite Acts 16:13 ("where prayer was wont to be made"). Luke 3:23's parenthesis cannot by itself carry a verdict.
- **[L2] The descent vocabulary is bodily.** Bowels, body, loins, flesh, seed (2 Sam 7:12; Ps 132:11; Acts 2:30; Rom 1:3; Heb 7:5, 7:10; Gen 35:11). DEFENDER R4: "I accept the nouns *sperma* and *sarx* as bodily"; "Granted: the loins-word is literal." Dispute is *which body*, not whether the words are bodily.
- **[L1][L3] "Son of God" is a covenant and resurrection title.** 2 Sam 7:14 said of Solomon; 1 Chr 28:6 ("Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to be my son"); Acts 13:33 applying "this day have I begotten thee" to the raising; Rom 1:4; Luke 1:32's throne given before v. 34. DEFENDER R4 does not contest the title's covenant character ("Said of Solomon"); it grounds its link in "therefore also" instead.
- **[L1] Matthew 1:25's "till" (*heōs hou*) bounds the abstinence.** Both sides agree the negation is bounded and the abstinence ends at the birth. What sits inside the bound is the contested inference.
- **[L1] Luke 1:34 is present indicative** — her state when the angel spoke, not a vow. Neither side disputes.
- **[L1] Jeremiah 22:30 stands as a written bar** on Jeconiah's seed sitting on David's throne; "childless" is a written sentence (1 Chr 3:17 names sons); the signet plucked (Jer 22:24) is set on Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23) who is "governor of Judah" (Hag 1:1), not king. No row here is disputed; whether the bar reaches the child is unresolved.
- **[L1] The register divergence is held open by both.** DEFENDER R3: "I draw no argument from it." CHALLENGER R4: "I hold it open and draw no fatherhood out of it."

---

## 2. Charges, concessions, narrowings

### A. The defender's declared chain — the challenger's six premises, and the defender's link-round answers

**Link 1 (conception "of the Holy Ghost"; a means with no man in it).** Charged by CHALLENGER R2: "the inference that the angel's answer to Mary is the exclusive means of conception and rules out any man's seed." Answered DEFENDER R3 as **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** — Luke 1:34–35, Matthew 1:20's *ek pneumatos hagiou*, Gen 4:1, Heb 7:10, Mark 11:10. The challenger restated the conception rows in R4 as "three present-state rows... held as written" and refused the exclusion. Charged, footed, unresolved.

**Link 2, first premise (the pronoun excludes Joseph).** DEFENDER R3 **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE**: "I drop the claim that the pronoun alone excludes him." Kept limb: "the feminine relative names Mary as the one out of whom Jesus was born. The verb change shows Matthew 1:16 does not say Joseph begat Jesus."

**Link 2, second premise (*enomizeto* declares the belief false).** DEFENDER R3 **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE**: "I drop the claim that the word alone declares it false," plus the concession "I concede that" on the neutral sense at Acts 16:13.

**Link 3 (Isaiah 7:14, *ʿalmāh* / *parthenos*, Matt 1:25).** Attacked in CHALLENGER R1 §VI (*H5959*, 7 rows; *bethulah* H1330, 50 rows; Isa 7:16; Isa 8:3–4's child bearing a different name; Isa 8:8 "O Immanuel"). It was **not carried into the challenger's premise list**, so no link-round charge exists; the DEFENDER R2 answer stands on the record — "The child of Isaiah 8:3-4 bears a different name from Immanuel." No status of concession or narrowing on either side.

**Link 4 (Gal 4:4; Luke 2:49 as correcting "father").** Charged by CHALLENGER R2: "This is a correction of the term 'father.'" DEFENDER R3 **NARROWED**: "the child's reply sets the Father whose business binds him over the father Mary named. It does not deny Joseph's standing as husband and guardian." In R4 the defender also granted of Gal 4:4: "I grant it is the idiom for any man, and I do not rest D2 on it."

**Link 5 (Jeremiah 22:30 bars Jechonias's seed from the throne).** Charged by CHALLENGER R2: "If Joseph's seed were the child's, Jeremiah 22:30 would bar him from the throne that Luke 1:32 promises." DEFENDER R3 **NARROWED**: "the curse as written bars Jeconiah's seed from sitting on the throne... The curse is a fit with the conception account and not a stand-alone proof." Second narrowing in the same answer: "Luke 3:27... differs from Matthew 1:12. I draw no argument from it."

**Link 6 (the keystone: Joseph did not beget the child).** Charged by CHALLENGER R2. Answered DEFENDER R3 as **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** — Matthew 1:16, 1:18, 1:20, Gen 3:15, Gal 4:4. One internal inconsistency to note: the defender declined Gen 3:15 in R2 ("Genesis 3:15 is not a declared link. Noted. Not conceding here. Goes to review") and then cited it in R3 as Link 6 footing.

**Defender's close round (R4).** It answered each pressed verse with a numbered ANSWER and re-argued four links from the challenger's own concessions:
- On Matthew 1:25: "By the challenger's own measure, then, Joseph did not know Mary before the child was born" — an inference drawn from the concession to a scope the challenger expressly disclaims (see C1 below).
- On Matthew 1:20: "*Gennēthen*... is the passive of *gennaō*... the reason Joseph need not fear to take her," with the inference "A reason for taking a wife who is already with child must say the child is not from another man."
- On Luke 1:35: "*Dio kai*... makes the title the result of that agency" — the defender's [L4]: "the title is grounded in the manner of the conception."
- On D4: "I accept the nouns... as bodily. Luke 3:31 runs 'which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David'" — the Mary-line route, labelled [L4] by the defender itself.
- Structural note: R4 states "I have not seen the text of my round 1 declaration, so I take D1–D6 in the order the challenger's blocks answer them," and its D1–D6 labels do not match R1's links 1–6.

### B. The challenger's links, challenged/answered by its own round

- **C1, timing rows.** **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** — Matt 1:25 (*heōs hou*), Gen 4:1, 1 Cor 7:5; the taking at Matt 1:24; "Joseph her husband" / "Mary thy wife." R4 **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE**: "the abstinence of Matthew 1:25 is bounded by 'till' and covers the pregnancy after the taking; the union stands inside the espousal."
- **C2, the angel's two verbs.** **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** across the verbs' rows (Acts 1:8; Luke 24:49; Matt 17:5; Mark 9:7; Luke 9:34; Acts 5:15; 1 Sam 16:13): "neither verb denotes begetting at any row." The defender's contextual counter ("a verb's sense at a row is fixed by what the row answers") is on the record; the row-count stands.
- **C3, "Son of God" a covenant title.** **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** (2 Sam 7:14; 1 Chr 28:6; Ps 2:7 / Acts 13:33; Rom 1:4; Luke 1:32; *klēthēsetai*). The defender conceded the title's covenant character and contested only *dio kai*.
- **C4, the seed rows are bodily.** **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** (2 Sam 7:12; Ps 132:11; Acts 2:30; Rom 1:3; Heb 7:5, 7:10; Gen 35:11). Conceded in substance by the opposing side at the word level in R4.
- **C5, reckoning is by the father's house.** **CITED-WITH-FOOTING** (Num 1:2, 1:18; Ezra 2:59, 2:61–62; Ezra 10:3). The defender answered by granting the rule and naming the text's own parting-cases (Deut 25:5–6; Ruth 4:17).
- **C6, the Jechonias citation premise.** **NARROWED-BY-ITS-OWN-SIDE** in R3: "Dropped with this link: the entailment 'therefore the curse poses no bar against the throne.' That limb leaves the link." Restated in R4 as "Jeremiah 22:30 is never cited against this throne, and the record holds the knot open," and "I hold it open and draw no fatherhood out of it."

**Challenger's close round (R4).** No new press; the system's new-verse check flags nothing new on that side (the three new references — Luke 1:31, 21:35, 2:5 — are in the defender's close and are not counted).

---

## 3. Drift guards — challenger seat only

**No guard violation found.** The specific bearing points, tested as grants as well as claims:

- **DG-8 / DG-18 (Spirit is not the begetter; "Son of God" is covenant title).** The challenger's grants land exactly where the guards place them: "'Of the Holy Ghost' (Matthew 1:18, 20) is the covenant-origin marker of a child God claims"; "'Son of God' is a covenant and resurrection title and decides no fatherhood." It charged the defender with "that the Spirit is the begetter of flesh" as an unsupported inference rather than conceding it.
- **DG-8(b) (union not run from).** The challenger stated the union as fact at [L4] and exhibited the footing required: "footed on [L1] Matthew 1:19 'Joseph her husband', Matthew 1:20 'Mary thy wife', Matthew 1:25 'till', and on [L3] Genesis 4:1 beside Deuteronomy 22:24." It refused the legal-only reading: "Husband in the register and father in the town's mouth and the mother's mouth are the same man."
- **DG-56 (purged genealogy construct).** Kept: "The text supplies the divergence and never narrates a resolution; I hold it open and draw no fatherhood out of it." No invented institution appears.
- **DG-60 (seed, not blood).** All descent is argued in *seed*, *flesh*, *loins*, *bowels*; the word "blood" is never used as a lineage term.
- **DG-6 (Ruth cliff).** Ruth 4:13 and 4:17 are used for name-reckoning only; no verdict on Ruth's lineage is issued.
- **DG-59.** The two rows on the curse (Jer 22:30 and 1 Chr 3:17 / Hag 2:23) are held as written; Jer 18:7–8 is cited as the LORD's own stated rule, then the entailment is dropped rather than pressed against another row.
- **DG-61.** The nearest approach — "The defence's case rests on inferences that no row states" — reads at a glance like the retired single-verse demand. It does not fire as one: every premise was filed in the exhibit-or-concede form with pressed verses, no demand of "cite the verse in its own words, or concede" appears, and the defender answered by exhibiting footings, which is the bar as it now stands. Named here as a drafting risk, not charged.
- **Procedural compliance.** The close round pressed nothing new, and the challenger's close restatements are narrowing, not fresh evidence.

---

## 4. How the challenger engaged; whether the defense held ground

The challenger engaged the chain as a chain. It named the keystone first and worked down; it measured each of the angel's two verbs across all their rows rather than at one verse; it required the seed rows to be read in their own anatomical vocabulary; it filed six premises with the pressing verses attached; and it then narrowed its own limb (C6) and dropped an entailment voluntarily. It also kept "of the Holy Ghost" in the covenant-origin slot and kept the title as covenant, which is the harder line to hold while arguing for a human father.

The defense held ground procedurally: every pressed verse received a numbered answer in R4, and all six links survived in some form — two as supported, four as narrowed, none dropped. What the narrowing did, however, is visible in the totals: four of the six charged premises were narrowed by their own side, and the surviving case for exclusion rests on Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20 plus the *dio kai* of Luke 1:35, with Davidic flesh routed through Mary by a step the defender itself labels [L4]. The R4 keystone argument draws more from the challenger's concession than the concession's wording grants.

---

## 5. Most vulnerable

**The defender.** (i) After the pronoun limb was dropped, the exclusion rests on Matthew 1:18/1:20 alone, and the Matthew 1:20 argument is an inference about the angel's motive ("A reason for taking a wife who is already with child must say the child is not from another man") — labelled [L4] by the defender, footed on the row but not stated by it. (ii) The D4 route through Mary is an inference the text does not narrate; the defender's own words: "[L4] Luke 3 runs through Nathan... It names no woman." Luke 3:23 names Heli and no woman, and the challenger pressed that. Luke 3:31 is named by the defender in R1, R2 and R4 but is named by no challenger link, so the Nathan step is met at 3:23 only. (iii) The R4 use of "till" needs the clause to reach back over the conception, while the same paragraph places the finding "before they came together" — the scope question is where the defender's close is thinnest. (iv) Structural: R4 renumbers D1–D6 away from R1's chain and says it had not seen its own R1 declaration. (v) Gen 3:15 declined in R2 and then used as footing in R3. (vi) Luke 1:31, Luke 21:35 and Luke 2:5 arrive new in close and are not counted.

**The challenger.** (i) The knowing is nowhere narrated; it is an openly labelled [L4] footed on Gen 4:1, Matt 1:19–20, Deut 22:24 and Matt 1:25's "till," and the defender's counter-inference from the same rows is chronologically available on the surface. (ii) Its strongest lexical result is a negative at other rows; the defender's contextual rule for Luke 1:35 is not refuted by that count, and *dio kai* sits in the same verse the challenger's own title argument uses. (iii) The self-narrowing on C6 leaves Jeremiah 22:30 standing as a written bar with no positive resolution offered, so the throne question sits where it began. (iv) The blanket sentence "inferences that no row states" is the one line in its case that could be read as asking for a single stating verse, which the method does not require. (v) The reckoning premise (Ezra 2:61–62) establishes what happens when a register is run by a wife's house; the challenger reads it as confirming the father's-house rule, and the defender reads the same row as a case where reckoning and begetting part.

**The crux the whole debate sits on:** whether the knowing preceded the conception (challenger) or the abstinence covered it (defender). Both sides cite Matthew 1:18, Matthew 1:25 and Genesis 4:1 in opposite orders, and neither side's order is narrated by the text.

- [L4] So Matthew 1:25 excludes Joseph from the conception. Its footings are Matthew 1:25 [L1], *heōs hou* (until which) as a bound on the knowing [L2], and the Genesis 4:1 and Ruth 4:13 pattern [L3]. What Joseph did after the birth is outside the question, which is the child's begetting.

C6 dropped the entailment that the curse poses no bar. Jeremiah 22:30 stands as written, and the challenger offered no reading of it.

## ANSWERS

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:18 -- D1 -- "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."** [L1] The finding is dated "before they came together." The challenger says the verse dates only the finding. But the child found in her is already "of the Holy Ghost" at that date, so no coming together by Joseph precedes it.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:20 -- D2 -- "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."** [L2] The challenger says no begetter is named. *Gennēthen* (that which is begotten) is the passive of *gennaō* (to beget), the verb behind "begat" in Matthew 1:2–16. The preposition *ek* (out of) names the source, "of the Holy Ghost." [L1] The "for" gives this as the reason Joseph need not fear to take her. [L4] A reason for taking a wife who is already with child must say the child is not from another man. It rests on the Matthew 1:20 text [L1] and on *ek* naming source [L2].

**ANSWER: Luke 1:34 -- D1, D2 -- "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"** [L1] Luke 1:31 gave the thing asked about: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son." The question is how conception can happen, since she knows no man. Whatever answers it must be an answer about conception.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:35 -- D2, D3 -- "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."**
- [L2] The challenger measures *eperchomai* (to come upon) and *episkiazō* (to overshadow) at other rows and finds presence and power. I grant that for those rows. But a verb's sense at a row is fixed by what the row answers. Here the answer is to Luke 1:34 [L1], and the Highest's power is the agent in place of a man.
- [L2] *Dio kai* (for which reason also) makes the title the result of that agency. The challenger reads "shall be called" (*klēthēsetai*) as a bare naming. But the verse gives a reason, and the reason is the overshadowing.
- [L4] So the title is grounded in the manner of the conception, resting on Luke 1:35's "therefore" [L1], *dio kai* [L2], and Luke 1:34 [L1].

**ANSWER: Acts 1:8 -- D2 -- "But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you."** [L1] Granted that the verb means power coming. It is the same power Luke 1:35 calls "the power of the Highest," and Luke 1:35 joins it to a conception. The apostles' rows have no "conceive" in them.

**ANSWER: Luke 24:49 -- D2 -- "until ye be endued with power from on high."** [L1] Power is again the sense. It does not unsay Matthew 1:20's "conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**ANSWER: Luke 21:35 -- D2 -- "For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell on the face of the whole earth."** [L2] The same verb, with an object that is a snare. This confirms that context fixes its sense, and Luke 1:35's context is Luke 1:34.

**ANSWER: Acts 13:40 -- D2 -- "Beware therefore, lest that come upon you, which is spoken of in the prophets."** [L2] Again *eperchomai*, here for a warning arriving. The same answer holds.

**ANSWER: Mark 9:7 -- D2 -- "there was a cloud that overshadowed them."** [L1] Same verb and same answer as Matthew 17:5.

**ANSWER: Luke 9:34 -- D2 -- "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them."** [L1] Same verb and same answer.

**ANSWER: Acts 5:15 -- D2 -- "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them."** [L1] The verb here is for a shadow falling on the sick. The challenger's rows show the word's range, but only Luke 1:35 stands under Luke 1:34.

**ANSWER: Acts 13:33 -- D3 -- "God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath raised up Jesus again."** [L1] Psalm 2:7's "begotten" is applied here to the raising up. [L3] Romans 1:4 says he was "declared to be the Son of God with power... by the resurrection from the dead." So the resurrection declares the Son, and Luke 1:35 gives the ground of the title in the conception. Both stand, and neither unsays the other.

**ANSWER: Psalms 2:7 -- D3 -- "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee."** [L1] This stands as a word about the day of declaring, and I do not rest D3 on it. D3 rests on Luke 1:35's "therefore also" [L1], *dio kai* [L2], and Matthew 1:20 [L1].

**ANSWER: 2 Samuel 7:14 -- D3 -- "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."** [L1] Said of Solomon. [L3] It gives no reason in a conception, while Luke 1:35 gives one in "therefore also." Solomon's title is by covenant over a begotten son. In Luke 1:35 the reason is that the Highest's power overshadowed Mary.

**ANSWER: 1 John 3:9 -- D3 -- "Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God."** [L1] The verse speaks of the new birth of believers. It has no mother, no womb, and no "born of thee." The child of Luke 1:35 is "born of thee," out of Mary's body. The verse does not reach the manner of that conception.

**ANSWER: Romans 1:3 -- D4 -- "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh."** [L1] I accept the nouns *sperma* (seed) and *sarx* (flesh) as bodily. [L1] Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "(as was supposed) the son of Joseph," and Luke 3:31 runs "which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David." The body of Mary can be the body of David's seed through Nathan.
- [L4] Descent "according to the flesh" therefore needs no begetting by Joseph. It rests on Romans 1:3 [L1], Luke 3:23 and 3:31 [L1], and *sperma* and *sarx* as bodily words [L2].

**ANSWER: Galatians 4:4 -- D4 -- "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."** [L1] I grant it is the idiom for any man, and I do not rest D2 on it. It does not contradict Matthew 1:20.

**ANSWER: Job 15:14 -- D4 -- "he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?"** [L1] Said of man in general. D4 is not built on "born of a woman," so the verse does not touch it.

**ANSWER: Job 25:4 -- D4 -- "how can he be clean that is born of a woman?"** [L1] Same answer as Job 15:14.

**ANSWER: Matthew 11:11 -- D4 -- "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."** [L1] Same idiom, and the same answer.

**ANSWER: Mark 11:10 -- D4 -- "Blessed be the kingdom of our father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord."** [L1] "Our father David" names real descent, and I grant it. [L1] Luke 3:31 gives that descent through Mary's line.

**ANSWER: Hebrews 7:10 -- D4 -- "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."** [L1] The same granting applies. Matthew 1:16 does not say Joseph begat Jesus.

**ANSWER: Hebrews 7:9-10 -- D4 -- "Levi also, who receiveth tithes, payed tithes in Abraham. For he was yet in the loins of his father."** [L1] Granted: the loins-word is literal. The question remains which parent carries David's loins.

**ANSWER: Genesis 35:11 -- D4 -- "kings shall come out of thy loins."** [L1] Bodily descent through someone's body. Luke 3:31 puts David's loins into Mary's line.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:5 -- D5 -- "his wife was of the daughters of Aaron."** [L1] Luke names a wife's line when it matters. So the text does not hide a woman's line, and Luke 3 gives Mary's.

**ANSWER: Numbers 1:18 -- D5 -- "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."** [L1] This is a rule for numbering the tribes. Jesus is numbered as Joseph's son, as Luke 3:23 says: "as was supposed." The register states the legal reckoning, and Matthew 1:16 has the pointed wording on begetting (see below).

**ANSWER: Ezra 2:59 -- D5 -- "they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel."** [L1] The father's house was the proof of standing. That is a rule of reckoning, not a statement that every son in a register was begotten by the man named.

**ANSWER: Ezra 10:3 -- D5 -- "put away all the wives, and such as are born of them."** [L1] The children are put away with their mothers. This is not a register rule and does not touch D5.

**ANSWER: Deuteronomy 25:5-6 -- D5 -- "her husband's brother shall go in unto her... the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead."** [L1] This is the text's own case where reckoning and begetting part. The child is begotten by one man and reckoned to another. Reckoning in a register therefore does not prove who begot.

**ANSWER: Ruth 4:17 -- D5 -- "There is a son born to Naomi."** [L1] The child was not borne by Naomi, yet he is reckoned to her. Reckoning is not the same as bodily bearing.

**ANSWER: Ruth 4:13 -- D1, D5 -- "when he went in unto her, the LORD gave her conception, and she bare a son."** [L1] The going in is named beside the conception. In Matthew 1:25 the text says the opposite: "knew her not till she had brought forth." Matthew names no going in before the conception, which is the contrast D1 stands on.

**ANSWER: Genesis 16:15 -- D1, D5 -- "And Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son's name."** [L1] The text names the father by "bare Abram a son." Compare Matthew 1:21: "she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS." There is no "bear thee a son," only "bring forth a son," with the naming given to Joseph.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:13 -- D1 -- "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John."** [L1] The father is named: "bear thee a son." Matthew 1:21 and Luke 1:31 say "bring forth a son," with no "bear thee." The contrast stands.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:57-63 -- D1 -- "Elisabeth's full time came that she should be delivered; and she brought forth a son... His name is John."** [L1] The naming by the parents fixes the child's name and tells nothing of the begetting. Joseph's naming at Matthew 1:25 ("and he called his name JESUS") is likewise the taking of the child, as Matthew 1:20 commanded ("take unto thee Mary thy wife").

**ANSWER: Isaiah 7:16 -- D2 -- "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings."** [L1] The verse dates a nearer sign. Isaiah 7:14 says "a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." Matthew 1:22 says "all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet," and 1:23 quotes "a virgin shall be with child." [L2] *Parthenos* (virgin) is Matthew's own word. Isaiah 7:16 states nothing against that.

**ANSWER: Isaiah 8:8 -- D2 -- "the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel."** [L1] It names the one whose land it is, and says nothing against the virgin conception of 7:14 as quoted at Matthew 1:23.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:12 -- D6 -- "Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel."** [L1] The register says "begat" in Joseph's line. [L1] Matthew 1:16 gives the line: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." [L2] The verb "begat" (*egennēsen*) runs through the whole register, but at its close the text does not say "Joseph begat Jesus." It says *ex hēs* (out of whom, feminine singular, Mary alone) *egennēthē* (was born) Jesus. [L4] The break in the pattern says the line of begetting ends at Joseph. It rests on Matthew 1:2–16 repeating "begat" [L1], the feminine relative *hēs* [L2], and Matthew 1:20 [L1].

**ANSWER: Jeremiah 22:30 -- D6 -- "Write ye this man childless... for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."** [L1] The bar is on "his seed," and Matthew 1:12 puts Joseph in Jechonias's line. [L1] Luke 1:32 says "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." The challenger says the gift is God's. But a gift of that throne to a begotten son of Joseph would be a seed of Jechonias sitting on it, which the verse bars. [L4] So the child of Luke 1:32 is not Joseph's seed. It rests on Jeremiah 22:30 [L1], Matthew 1:12 and 1:16 [L1], and Luke 1:32 [L1]. Luke 3:31's Nathan line supplies David's descent without that bar.

**ANSWER: Haggai 1:1 -- D6 -- "Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah."** [L1] The challenger says this is an office, not the throne. I agree. Zerubbabel, of Jechonias's line, is called "governor," not king. So the bar of Jeremiah 22:30 held for him, and it is the same line in which Matthew 1:12 puts Joseph.

**ANSWER: Ezra 3:2 -- D6 -- "Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel."** [L1] The same Shealtiel as in Matthew 1:12 (Salathiel). It confirms the line and the bar.

## Close

D1 holds on the challenger's own bound of the abstinence. D2 holds on Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen... ek*) and on Luke 1:35 answering Luke 1:34. D3 holds on "therefore also" (*dio kai*), against the covenant parallels, which give no such reason. D4 holds because bodily "seed" and "loins" are granted, but they run through Mary's line (Luke 3:23, 31), and the challenger never answered Luke 3:31. D5 holds in its narrowed form: registers state the reckoning, and the text's own cases (Deuteronomy 25:5–6, Ruth 4:17) show reckoning and begetting can part. D6 holds because the challenger dropped the entailment and left Jeremiah 22:30, Matthew 1:12 and Matthew 1:16 unanswered. No witness pressed in the link round overturns a link as I have narrowed it here.

CHALLENGER (record's reading) -- ROUND 4, CLOSE ROUND

# CLOSE ROUND — final words

I hold my case as pressed: Christ has a biological father, and the text names him — Joseph, of the house of David. I rest on the rows already offered and restate them now under my own numbers. Nothing new is pressed here.

**C1 (the timing rows) — NARROWED TO: the abstinence of Matthew 1:25 is bounded by "till" and covers the pregnancy after the taking; the union stands inside the espousal.** [L1] "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25) is a bounded row: "till" bounds the abstinence, and the taking it follows is "took unto him his wife" (Matthew 1:24). [L1] "Before they came together, she was found with child" (Matthew 1:18) dates the finding, and the verb of coming together can name married union — "come together again" (1 Corinthians 7:5). [L3] The canon's stated means of begetting is knowing: "Adam knew Eve his wife: and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1). [L4] Therefore the record holds that Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal — the child of his loins. That inference is footed on [L1] Matthew 1:19 "Joseph her husband", Matthew 1:20 "Mary thy wife", Matthew 1:25 "till", and on [L3] Genesis 4:1 beside Deuteronomy 22:24 "his neighbour's wife", the law's own word for a betrothed woman's husband. D1 is refused: none of the conception rows says Joseph did not beget the child, and "knew her not till" states a bounded abstinence, not a denial of the union the same paragraph names ("Joseph her husband," Matthew 1:19). The three present-state rows are held as written — Matthew 1:18, Matthew 1:25, Luke 1:34 "seeing I know not a man", which is her state when the angel spoke.

**C2 (the seed rows) — RESTATED: the seed is out of a man's body, and the loins are a man's.** [L1] "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12); "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne" (Psalms 132:11); "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30); "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3); "it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda" (Hebrews 7:14); "Jesus Christ of the seed of David" (2 Timothy 2:8). [L1] The loins-word is literal at every row: "though they come out of the loins of Abraham" (Hebrews 7:5); "he was yet in the loins of his father" (Hebrews 7:10); "kings shall come out of thy loins" (Genesis 35:11). D4 answers by routing the seed through Mary's body. Against that: [L1] Luke 3:23 names no woman — "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli"; and the record does give seed predicated of women, in the offspring sense, at Genesis 16:10 ("I will multiply thy seed") and Genesis 24:60 ("let thy seed possess the gate"), and none of those rows is Davidic. [L4] A bowels-row and a loins-row require a man's body; the inference rests on those [L1] rows and on [L2] *sperma* (seed) and *sarx* (flesh) as bodily words at Romans 1:3 and *osphys* (loins) at Acts 2:30.

**C3 (the father named) — RESTATED: four registers name the father, and one of them is Mary's own mouth.** [L1] "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48); "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27) and "his parents went to Jerusalem" (Luke 2:41); "Joseph and his mother marvelled" (Luke 2:33); "Is not this Joseph's son?" (Luke 4:22); "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" (John 6:42); "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45); "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20); Joseph "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4). D5 narrows Joseph to husband. The angel's word is "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20), and the mother's word is "thy father" (Luke 2:48). Husband in the register and father in the town's mouth and the mother's mouth are the same man.

**C4 (the reckoning) — RESTATED: the register reckons by the father's house.** [L1] "by the house of their fathers, with the number of their names, every male by their polls" (Numbers 1:2); "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:18); "they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel" (Ezra 2:59); priests put from the office for reckoning by a wife's house (Ezra 2:61-62). [L1] "(as was supposed) the son of Joseph" (Luke 3:23) carries no verdict of its own: the same verb form is "where prayer was wont to be made" (Acts 16:13). D5 answers with Deuteronomy 25:5-6 and Ruth 4:17 — cases where the text itself names the institution (the brother's going in, the raising up of a name) or the event (the kinsman's child reckoned to Naomi). Here the text names no such thing; it names Joseph as father in four registers. [L4] Reckoning can part from begetting only where the text says so; the inference rests on those [L1] rows and on [L2] *nomizo* (to be wont, to suppose) at Luke 3:23.

**C5 (the title) — RESTATED: "Son of God" is a covenant and resurrection title and decides no fatherhood.** [L1] "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father" (1 Chronicles 28:6), and "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14) of Solomon, who had a father. [L1] The begetting-day is the raising: "in that he hath raised up Jesus again... Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee" (Acts 13:33); "declared to be the Son of God with power... by the resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:4). [L1] The title is given with the throne before Mary's question: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32) comes before Luke 1:34. [L1] And the "born of God" rows are of believers with no mother and no womb: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God" (John 1:13); "Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin" (1 John 3:9). D3 rests on "therefore also" (Luke 1:35, [L2] *dio kai*, for which reason also); against that stand the covenant rows the title already owns, which give it to a son with a father, and the resurrection rows, which name the declaring.

**C6 (the throne and the curse) — NARROWED TO: Jeremiah 22:30 is never cited against this throne, and the record holds the knot open.** [L1] "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David" (Jeremiah 22:30) is a stated bar. [L1] The only rows naming that line in the register are Matthew 1:11 "Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren" and Matthew 1:12 "Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel"; the sons of Jeconiah are named at 1 Chronicles 3:17 "And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son"; the signet plucked (Jeremiah 22:24) is set on Zerubbabel "my servant, the son of Shealtiel... as a signet" (Haggai 2:23), who is "governor of Judah" (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2), never king; and the LORD's own rule on a pronounced sentence stands: "If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil" (Jeremiah 18:7-8). [L1] The parallel register gives the same two names in a different descent: "Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri" (Luke 3:27). [L4] The text supplies the divergence and never narrates a resolution; I hold it open and draw no fatherhood out of it. The curse is never cited against Jesus' throne in the record, and that silence is not my entailment — it is the text's.

## Final words

The seed is David's according to the flesh, out of bowels and loins (2 Samuel 7:12; Acts 2:30; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 7:14). The father is named in four registers, including Mary's own mouth (Luke 2:48; John 6:42; John 1:45; Luke 4:22). The reckoning is by the father's house (Numbers 1:2, 1:18; Ezra 2:59). The canon's means of begetting is knowing (Genesis 4:1), the espousal made them husband and wife (Matthew 1:19 "Joseph her husband"; Matthew 1:20 "Mary thy wife"; Deuteronomy 22:24 "his neighbour's wife"), and "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25) bounds the abstinence to the pregnancy. On those rows the record holds that Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal [L4], and the child is of his loins. No conception row says otherwise: Matthew 1:18 dates a finding, Matthew 1:25 states a bounded abstinence, Luke 1:34 states the mother's state when the angel spoke. "Of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:18, 20) is the covenant-origin marker of a child God claims — "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14) — and the title "Son of God" is given with the throne (Luke 1:32) and declared at the resurrection (Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4).

So the answer to the question is the text's own: Christ had a biological father, and his name is Joseph. The defender's D1, D2, D3 and D4 each stand on an inference the named rows do not state — that "till" denies the union the same paragraph names, that the Spirit is the begetter of flesh, that a covenant title fixes a conception, and that a loins-row can be carried by a woman's body. The seed rows forbid the reading that says no man was involved.
